meta.blurb: Our two best theories of nature work brilliantly, yet they clash inside a black hole. String theory is a bold, unproven idea about tiny vibrating loops that might bring them together. It says plainly what we know and what we do not.
meta.bible: Voice: clear, curious and honest, speaking to "you". The science is real; string theory is not proven, and the text says so wherever it matters. Plan: relativity, then quantum physics, then the clash between them, then string theory, then the doubts and the open questions. chapters: A Loop Instead of a Point

beats.scene: A person lies on a hill at night looking at stars and the Moon
beats.summary: You ask what space and time are made of, and the book sets out its plan.

beats.scene: A shepherd, a stone calendar and a line of stars over a field
beats.summary: For thousands of years people watched the sky and found it regular, like a clock.

beats.scene: A man with a small telescope points it at four dots beside Jupiter
beats.summary: In 1610 Galileo saw moons around Jupiter and showed that motion is not simple.

beats.scene: A great empty stage with a clock and a ruler standing on it
beats.summary: Newton described space as a fixed stage and time as a clock ticking the same for all.

beats.scene: An apple falling beside a tree while the Moon hangs in the sky
beats.summary: The same pull that drops an apple also keeps the Moon circling Earth.

beats.scene: Three balls at different distances from a big planet with arrows of different sizes
beats.summary: Gravity grows weaker with distance: twice as far means a pull four times weaker.

beats.scene: A comet with a long tail swings round the Sun above old charts
beats.summary: Newton's rules predicted tides and the return of a comet, all in the right year.

beats.scene: An astronomer at a desk covered with sums beside a telescope at night
beats.summary: In 1846 maths alone pointed to an unseen planet, Neptune, and it was found.

beats.scene: An orbit drawn as a slowly turning oval around the Sun
beats.summary: Mercury's orbit shifted slightly more than Newton's rules said it should.

beats.scene: A reader at a crossroads with signs for relativity, quantum and strings
beats.summary: Nobody knew how gravity crosses empty space, and this book sets out three steps.

beats.scene: An astronomer times a moon vanishing behind Jupiter on a night in 1676
beats.summary: In 1676 Rømer used the timing of Jupiter's moons to show that light takes time to travel.

beats.scene: A beam of light crossing from Earth to the Moon beside a stopwatch
beats.summary: Light moves at about three hundred thousand kilometres a second, taking eight minutes from the Sun.

beats.scene: A magnet and a wire with glowing waves spreading from them
beats.summary: In the 1860s Maxwell showed that electricity and magnetism make waves that move at the speed of light.

beats.scene: An invisible sea drawn around the Earth as it moves through it
beats.summary: Waves seemed to need something to wave in, so scientists imagined an invisible ether.

beats.scene: Two beams of light at right angles bouncing off mirrors on a stone table
beats.summary: In 1887 Michelson and Morley looked for the ether and found no sign of it.

beats.scene: Scientists around a blackboard crossing out sums and arguing
beats.summary: Some tried odd fixes to save the ether, but the puzzle stayed.

beats.scene: A teenage boy in a field imagines running beside a beam of light
beats.summary: As a teenager Einstein wondered what it would be like to race a beam of light.

beats.scene: A young man sits at a high desk in a small office with papers
beats.summary: In 1905, working as a patent clerk in Bern, Einstein found two simple ideas to guide him.

beats.scene: A runner and a train both watching the same beam of light go by
beats.summary: A thrown ball adds its speed to the train's, but light does not.

beats.scene: A beam of light stays the same length as a runner stops behind it
beats.summary: Einstein kept the rule about light and changed what we think of space and time.

beats.scene: A glass tube with a flash of light bouncing between two mirrors
beats.summary: A light clock ticks each time a flash bounces between two mirrors.

beats.scene: A moving light clock with the flash tracing a long zigzag path
beats.summary: If the clock moves, the flash travels a longer path, so each tick takes longer.

beats.scene: A slow car and a fast rocket, each with a clock on its dashboard
beats.summary: The slowing is tiny at everyday speeds and dramatic near the speed of light.

beats.scene: A small particle falls from a cloud to a detector on the ground
beats.summary: Muons from the sky reach the ground in great numbers because their clocks run slow.

beats.scene: An aeroplane carrying an atomic clock beside a matching clock on the ground
beats.summary: In 1971 clocks flown round the world disagreed by the amount predicted.

beats.scene: A fast spaceship looks squashed in its direction of travel
beats.summary: A moving object is shorter along its direction of motion.

beats.scene: A train with lightning striking both ends, seen by two different observers
beats.summary: Whether two events happen at the same time depends on who is watching.

beats.scene: A rocket pushing hard but gaining less and less speed near a glowing line
beats.summary: Pushing a mass ever closer to light speed takes ever more energy, so it never gets there.

beats.scene: Two twins, one on a rocket leaving Earth and one waving from the ground
beats.summary: A traveller who flies fast and returns can be younger than a twin who stayed.

beats.scene: Two observers each holding a clock and each looking at the other's clock
beats.summary: Each observer sees the other's clock slow, and both are right.

beats.scene: A bearded teacher at a blackboard draws a grid of space and time lines
beats.summary: In 1908 the mathematician Minkowski showed that relativity joins space and time into one four-dimensional spacetime.

beats.scene: A calendar page, a street map and a tall building with a marked window
beats.summary: To fix an event you need four numbers: three for where and one for when.

beats.scene: A chart with time running upward and a vertical line for someone standing still
beats.summary: On a spacetime map, every object draws a line through time, called its worldline.

beats.scene: Two observers draw different grids on the same sheet of events
beats.summary: Different observers cut spacetime into space and time differently, but they agree on deeper facts.

beats.scene: A glowing double cone with a bright event at its tip
beats.summary: Light draws a cone around each event, marking what can reach it and what it can affect.

beats.scene: A signal arrives inside a glowing cone while a flash outside stays silent
beats.summary: Cause comes before effect for everyone, and events outside the cone cannot affect each other.

beats.scene: A tiny glowing speck inside a heavy block with a large flame beside it
beats.summary: Mass is a form of stored energy, and a little mass is worth a vast amount of energy.

beats.scene: The Sun shines in the dark as tiny grains of matter become light
beats.summary: The Sun turns about four million tonnes of matter into light every second.

beats.scene: A nuclear power station beside a heap of fuel pellets and a lamp
beats.summary: Splitting heavy atoms turns a tiny part of their mass into heat and power.

beats.scene: A collider ring with a burst of new glowing particles from a head-on crash
beats.summary: In colliders energy becomes new particles, and most of a proton's mass is energy itself.

beats.scene: A man at a desk looks out at a roof
beats.summary: In 1907 Einstein pictured a man falling freely and saw that he would not feel his own weight.

beats.scene: A closed lift floating in space and another resting on the ground
beats.summary: Inside a closed lift, you cannot tell gravity from steady acceleration.

beats.scene: A beam of light crossing a rising lift and bending as it goes
beats.summary: If acceleration bends light, then gravity must bend light as well.

beats.scene: A globe with two flight paths and a flat map beside it
beats.summary: On a curved surface the shortest paths look curved when drawn on a flat map.

beats.scene: A man and his friend bent over thick books of curved geometry
beats.summary: Einstein spent eight years finding the mathematics for curved spacetime, with help from a friend.

beats.scene: A heavy ball on a stretched sheet with a small marble circling it
beats.summary: A mass bends spacetime around it, and objects follow the straightest paths through the bend.

beats.scene: Clocks on a high floor and a low floor showing different times
beats.summary: Time runs slower where gravity is stronger, so spacetime bends in time as well as space.

beats.scene: An astronomer smiles at an oval orbit that now matches the sums exactly
beats.summary: In 1915 the new theory explained Mercury's orbit exactly, and Einstein was delighted.

beats.scene: Two physicists beside a tall tower with a detector at each end
beats.summary: In 1959 an experiment on a tower showed that light changes as it climbs against gravity.

beats.scene: A satellite above Earth and a phone showing a map
beats.summary: GPS satellites must correct for both kinds of time change, or maps would drift.

beats.scene: A star's light bending in an arc past the edge of the Sun
beats.summary: General relativity predicted that the Sun bends starlight by twice the amount Newton's rules gave.

beats.scene: Astronomers with cameras under a dark sky during a total eclipse
beats.summary: In 1919 expeditions photographed stars during an eclipse to test the bending.

beats.scene: A newspaper front page with a thoughtful man's picture and a bold headline
beats.summary: The results of the eclipse made Einstein famous around the world.

beats.scene: A cluster of galaxies bending distant light into bright arcs and rings
beats.summary: Heavy galaxies act as lenses, bending light from far behind them into arcs and rings.

beats.scene: An old scholar sketches a star so heavy that its light is trapped
beats.summary: In the 1780s thinkers had imagined stars so heavy that light could not leave.

beats.scene: A soldier at a desk in a trench writing equations by lamplight
beats.summary: In 1916 Schwarzschild solved Einstein's equations for a single round mass.

beats.scene: A dark sphere with a measuring line from its centre to its edge
beats.summary: The solution has a critical distance inside which light cannot get out, about three kilometres for the Sun's mass.

beats.scene: A great star collapsing inward into a small dark ball
beats.summary: A heavy star at the end of its life can collapse into a black hole, bounded by an event horizon.

beats.scene: A traveller stretches out as she falls toward a dark sphere
beats.summary: Falling into a black hole stretches a body, and from outside the fall looks endlessly slow.

beats.scene: A glowing orange ring around a black centre in a computer image
beats.summary: Evidence for black holes has grown, from stars at our galaxy's centre to the first picture in 2019.

beats.scene: A sheet of fabric with ripples spreading out from two small weights
beats.summary: In 1916 Einstein predicted gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime that move at the speed of light.

beats.scene: Two small stars circling each other, with a chart of a shrinking orbit
beats.summary: A pair of stars in the 1970s lost energy exactly as gravitational waves would take it.

beats.scene: A huge L-shaped building in a field with long pipes and a laser
beats.summary: LIGO uses two huge L-shaped detectors with laser beams four kilometres long.

beats.scene: A computer screen showing a short rising squeal of a wave pattern
beats.summary: On 14 September 2015 LIGO heard a short chirp from far away.

beats.scene: Two black holes spiral together while ripples spread across a grid
beats.summary: The chirp came from two black holes that merged more than a billion years ago, far away.

beats.scene: Two small neutron stars colliding in a flash of gold and light
beats.summary: More signals followed, including in 2017 the merger of two neutron stars.

beats.scene: A scientist adds a weight to hold a model universe still
beats.summary: Einstein's equations said the Universe could not stand still, but he added a term to hold it steady.

beats.scene: A balloon with dots drawn on it grows larger as the dots move apart
beats.summary: In 1929 Hubble found that distant galaxies move away, the farther the faster.

beats.scene: A film running backward as a vast space shrinks to a bright dense point
beats.summary: Run backward, expansion leads to a hot, dense start about fourteen billion years ago.

beats.scene: A telescope dish beside a faint glow of colours across a dark sky
beats.summary: In 1998 astronomers found the expansion is speeding up, and no one knows why.

beats.scene: A glowing hot poker in a dark workshop with a graph of light colours
beats.summary: Old physics wrongly predicted that a hot object should glow with endless blue light.

beats.scene: A scientist at a desk in 1900 writing sums with a puzzled look
beats.summary: In 1900 Planck solved the puzzle by supposing that energy comes in small packets.

beats.scene: Small packets of blue light and smaller packets of red light in a row
beats.summary: The size of a packet depends on the colour, and the packets are extremely small.

beats.scene: Blue light knocking sparks from a metal plate while red light does nothing
beats.summary: Light shone on metal knocks out electrons, but only if its colour is right.

beats.scene: A beam of light drawn as a stream of tiny bright dots
beats.summary: In 1905 Einstein said that light itself comes in packets, now called photons.

beats.scene: Water waves from two sources crossing and making a striped pattern
beats.summary: Light also makes wave patterns, so it acts as both a wave and a particle.

beats.scene: A tiny dense centre with an electron falling toward it in a spiral
beats.summary: Rutherford found that atoms have a tiny heavy centre, but old rules said electrons should crash into it.

beats.scene: An atom with rings around its nucleus and an electron hopping between rings
beats.summary: In 1913 Bohr said that electrons sit in fixed levels and give out light when they jump.

beats.scene: A prism splitting starlight into coloured lines with dark gaps
beats.summary: Each element has its own pattern of coloured lines, which tells us what stars are made of.

beats.scene: An electron beam making rings on a screen like a wave of light
beats.summary: In 1924 de Broglie suggested that matter acts like waves, and experiments agreed.

beats.scene: Two young scientists in different cities writing equations on paper
beats.summary: In 1925 and 1926 Heisenberg and Schrödinger found two new forms of quantum physics that agreed.

beats.scene: A smooth wave of cloud shape spreading above a map with one small mark
beats.summary: Schrödinger's wave describes the electron, and Born showed that it gives only the odds of finding it.

beats.scene: A screen with two narrow slits and a striped pattern forming from small dots
beats.summary: Single electrons fired through two slits slowly build up a wave pattern.

beats.scene: A detector beside one slit and two plain bands on the screen
beats.summary: If you check which slit each electron uses, the wave pattern disappears.

beats.scene: A young man with a notebook in a quiet northern town at night
beats.summary: In 1927 Heisenberg showed that position and motion cannot both be exactly known.

beats.scene: A splash on a pond beside a long smooth wave, both marked with rulers
beats.summary: A short wave has a clear place but an unclear length, which is the root of the limit.

beats.scene: An electron drawn as a blur of many places that sharpens into one dot
beats.summary: Before it is measured, a particle can be in several states, and a measurement gives one.

beats.scene: Two men in old suits arguing across a table in a crowded hotel
beats.summary: Einstein did not like chance at the heart of nature, and Bohr defended the new theory.

beats.scene: A cat in a closed box with two glowing outcomes drawn above it
beats.summary: In 1935 Schrödinger invented a cat that was alive and dead to show how strange this seemed.

beats.scene: Three doors labelled with different pictures of the same experiment
beats.summary: Scientists still disagree about what quantum physics means, though all agree about its predictions.

beats.scene: A man at a blackboard joins two equations with a large bracket
beats.summary: In 1928 Dirac joined quantum physics with special relativity in a single equation for the electron.

beats.scene: A cloud chamber photograph with a curved track starting from a lead plate
beats.summary: The equation predicted antimatter, and in 1932 the positron was found.

beats.scene: A calm sheet of fabric with small ripples spreading in different places
beats.summary: In quantum field theory, particles are ripples in fields that fill all space.

beats.scene: Wavy lines and arrows joining at points on a page of simple diagrams
beats.summary: Feynman's pictures helped calculate how electrons and light interact, to astonishing accuracy.

beats.scene: A tiny glow of energy flickering in a dark box said to be empty
beats.summary: Empty space is never quiet, and the small shift measured in 1947 showed it.

beats.scene: Two glowing particles far apart on either side of a dark space
beats.summary: Einstein and two colleagues pointed out in 1935 that quantum particles can be strongly linked.

beats.scene: Two detectors with matching results on a screen in two distant rooms
beats.summary: In 1964 Bell found a test, and experiments since have shown the links are real.

beats.scene: A hand holding a phone with a stop sign across a path of light
beats.summary: Entanglement cannot be used to send messages faster than light.

beats.scene: A laser beam, a computer chip and a medical scanner on a table
beats.summary: Quantum physics gave us lasers, transistors, computer chips and medical scanners.

beats.scene: A satellite, an atomic clock and a solar panel under a bright sun
beats.summary: Atomic clocks, LEDs and solar cells depend on quantum rules, and quantum computers are being built.

beats.scene: Four arrows of different colours pointing from a small circle
beats.summary: Nature has four forces: gravity, electromagnetism, and the strong and weak forces.

beats.scene: Two skaters throw a ball back and forth and slide apart
beats.summary: Each of three forces is carried by its own messenger particle, such as the photon.

beats.scene: A tiny three-part knot inside a larger glowing ball
beats.summary: Protons and neutrons are made of smaller particles called quarks, which never appear alone.

beats.scene: A stream of faint ghostly dots passing through a person and the ground
beats.summary: Neutrinos are very light particles that pass through ordinary matter almost without a trace.

beats.scene: Three rows of small glowing balls, each row heavier than the last
beats.summary: Matter particles come in three families, and nobody knows why.

beats.scene: A table of small glowing balls grouped by colour and size
beats.summary: The Standard Model lists the known particles and is tested to astonishing accuracy.

beats.scene: A glowing sea filling a dark room with small particles wading through it
beats.summary: The Higgs field gives mass to particles, and a ripple of it is the Higgs boson.

beats.scene: A huge ring of machinery underground with two beams meeting in the middle
beats.summary: In 2012 the Higgs boson was found at the Large Hadron Collider.

beats.scene: A list of three forces with an empty space left for a fourth
beats.summary: The Standard Model leaves out gravity.

beats.scene: A pie chart with a small slice of ordinary matter and large dark slices
beats.summary: Dark matter, dark energy and the lack of antimatter show the model is incomplete.

beats.scene: A smooth sheet on the left beside a jittering fuzzy sheet on the right
beats.summary: Relativity describes smooth spacetime, while quantum physics describes a jumpy, uncertain world.

beats.scene: A tiny atom and a huge planet at opposite ends of a long road
beats.summary: Usually the two theories do not meet, because gravity is weak for small things.

beats.scene: A tiny particle labelled graviton passing between two glowing masses
beats.summary: If gravity works like other forces, tiny messengers called gravitons should carry it.

beats.scene: A page of equations ending with an endless line of numbers
beats.summary: When the sums include gravitons at tiny distances, the answers become infinite and useless.

beats.scene: A ruler shrinks from a person to a cell, an atom and a dot
beats.summary: The Planck length is the tiny scale at which quantum gravity should matter.

beats.scene: A calm sea seen from far above and rough bubbling foam up close
beats.summary: John Wheeler pictured spacetime as seething foam at the smallest scale.

beats.scene: A dark point inside a black hole beside a tiny glowing dot
beats.summary: At a black hole's centre, relativity predicts infinite density, and the theory breaks down.

beats.scene: A film strip running backward to a tiny glowing point
beats.summary: At the Big Bang everything was squeezed small and dense, and the same breakdown appears.

beats.scene: A black hole slowly shrinking while a faint glow leaves its edge
beats.summary: In 1974 Hawking showed that black holes glow faintly and slowly shrink, raising a puzzle.

beats.scene: Two puzzle pieces that do not fit, with a gap between them
beats.summary: A new theory is needed that fits relativity and quantum physics together.

beats.scene: A young theorist in 1968 holds a page from an old maths book
beats.summary: In 1968 Veneziano found an old mathematical formula that matched strong force data.

beats.scene: Three physicists sketch a small vibrating loop on a board
beats.summary: In 1970 three physicists saw that the formula describes tiny vibrating strings.

beats.scene: A crossed-out board with quarks written beside a rubbed-out loop
beats.summary: A better theory of the strong force, based on quarks, took over in the 1970s.

beats.scene: A strange extra particle glows on a table next to a gravity sign
beats.summary: In 1974 Scherk and Schwarz saw that the unwanted particle was the graviton.

beats.scene: A lone physicist working late with a small stack of papers
beats.summary: John Schwarz kept working on the idea for ten years while most people ignored it.

beats.scene: Crowds of young physicists in a lecture hall in 1984
beats.summary: In 1984 Green and Schwarz removed a fatal flaw, and the field exploded.

beats.scene: A far coin looks like a dot, a near coin shows its ring
beats.summary: The core idea is to replace a point-like particle with a tiny loop of string.

beats.scene: A ruler zooming in from a person to an atom to a loop
beats.summary: A string is so small, about the Planck length, that it looks like a point.

beats.scene: A glowing loop on its own with no smaller pieces inside
beats.summary: A string is not made of anything smaller, but is the basic ingredient itself.

beats.scene: A single thread weaving into the shapes of many different particles
beats.summary: If it is right, all matter and forces come from one kind of thing.

beats.scene: A guitar string vibrating in several different shapes above a sound hole
beats.summary: A guitar string can vibrate in many patterns, and each pattern is a different note.

beats.scene: A glowing loop with different wave patterns next to labels for particles
beats.summary: Each vibration pattern of a string would be a different particle.

beats.scene: A calm loop beside a small weight, a shaking loop beside a large one
beats.summary: A faster vibration carries more energy, so it gives a heavier particle.

beats.scene: A tight string pulled hard between two huge mountains
beats.summary: Strings are pulled so tight that almost all patterns are far too heavy to see.

beats.scene: An open piece of string beside a closed ring with a wave
beats.summary: Strings can be open pieces or closed loops, and a closed loop includes the graviton.

beats.scene: Two loops merging into one and then splitting into two again
beats.summary: Strings can split and join, and these are the interactions of the theory.

beats.scene: A smooth glowing tube joining two circles, with no sharp corner anywhere
beats.summary: Because strings join smoothly, there is no single point where the sums explode.

beats.scene: A rubber band cannot be squeezed into a point between two fingers
beats.summary: Because a string has size, it may smooth out the wild jumps of tiny spacetime.

beats.scene: Two kinds of loops, one with fine arrows and one with wavy lines
beats.summary: Adding supersymmetry gives the theory matter as well as forces, and the name superstring.

beats.scene: A control panel with all its dials missing and one blank space
beats.summary: In principle string theory has no adjustable numbers, which makes it very demanding.

beats.scene: A letter from a young scholar to Einstein, with a drawing of five axes
beats.summary: In 1919 Kaluza proposed a fifth dimension that could join gravity and electromagnetism.

beats.scene: A flat sheet whose edge rolls into a tiny tube
beats.summary: In 1926 Klein suggested that the extra dimension is curled up too small to see.

beats.scene: An ant on a garden hose, seen far away and then close up
beats.summary: From far a hose looks like a line, but up close it has a small circle to walk around.

beats.scene: A blackboard where the sums only work when the number ten is written
beats.summary: The maths of superstrings works only in ten dimensions of spacetime, nine of space and one of time.

beats.scene: A tiny six-sided knot drawn at every point of a larger grid
beats.summary: The six extra dimensions may be rolled up into a shape too small to see.

beats.scene: Two mathematicians in front of a twisted, folded shape with many loops
beats.summary: Calabi-Yau shapes were proposed in 1985 as possible hidden dimensions.

beats.scene: A trumpet with a different bell shape beside a set of sound waves
beats.summary: The shape of the hidden dimensions would decide which particles and forces exist.

beats.scene: A great library of different glowing shapes, each with its own label
beats.summary: There is an enormous number of possible shapes, and no one knows which is ours.

beats.scene: A tiny gap between two plates with a delicate meter measuring a force
beats.summary: Experiments on gravity at tiny distances have so far found no sign of extra dimensions.

beats.scene: A traveller at a signpost that points in directions that cannot be seen
beats.summary: Hidden dimensions come from the mathematics, and there is no direct evidence for them.

beats.scene: Five slightly different glowing loops side by side on a lecture table
beats.summary: By the late 1980s there were five different superstring theories, which was an embarrassment.

beats.scene: A small circle and a large circle that give the same result
beats.summary: Dualities showed that a string on a very large circle matches one on a very small circle.

beats.scene: Two linked panels, one marked strong and one marked weak
beats.summary: Some pairs of theories turn out to be one theory seen at strong and weak strength.

beats.scene: A man at a podium before a screen with five lines joining
beats.summary: In 1995 Witten argued that the five theories are parts of one deeper theory, called M-theory.

beats.scene: A circle that grows into a cylinder as an extra dimension appears

In 1907, Einstein saw that a falling person does not feel any weight.

People later found more waves, even from two small dead stars.
Einstein thought the Universe stays the same size, so he changed his sums.

If we go back in time, the Universe was once very hot and small.
In 1998, people found that the Universe is growing faster and faster.
Old physics said that a hot object should give out endless blue light.

When light hits metal, it can knock out tiny pieces called electrons.

Light also makes patterns like water waves, so it acts like both.
Atoms have a tiny heavy centre, but the electrons should fall into it.
In 1913, Niels Bohr said that electrons stay in fixed levels around the atom.
Each kind of atom gives out its own special colours of light.
In 1924, a French prince said that matter can behave like a wave.
In 1925 and 1926, two young men found new ways to do quantum physics.
Schrödinger's wave tells us the chance of finding an electron somewhere.
When we fire single electrons at two slits, they slowly make a wave pattern.
If we watch which slit the electron uses, the pattern goes away.
In 1927, Heisenberg said that we cannot know position and motion exactly together.
A short wave shows a clear place, but its length is not clear.
Before we measure it, an electron can be in many states at once.
Einstein did not like chance in nature, but Bohr said it was real.
Schrödinger imagined a cat that was both alive and dead to show the problem.
People still argue about what quantum physics means, but the sums always work.
In 1928, Paul Dirac joined quantum physics and relativity in one equation.
His equation said that antimatter must exist, and people found it in 1932.
In quantum field theory, particles are small ripples in fields that fill space.
Richard Feynman drew simple pictures to show how light and electrons meet.
Empty space is never still, and experiments have shown this.
In 1935, Einstein pointed out that two particles can stay strongly linked.
In 1964, John Bell found a test, and later experiments showed the link is real.
You cannot use these links to send a message faster than light.
Quantum physics gave us lasers, computer chips and machines that scan the body.
Quantum rules also run atomic clocks, LED lamps and solar panels.
Nature has four forces, and two of them work inside atoms.
Each force has a messenger particle, and light is the messenger of one.
Protons and neutrons are made of smaller particles called quarks.
Neutrinos are tiny particles that pass through your body all day long.
Matter particles come in three families, and nobody knows why.
A short list called the Standard Model names all the known particles.
The Higgs field gives particles their mass, like a thick sea around them.
In 2012, scientists found the Higgs particle in a huge machine near Geneva.
The Standard Model is very good, but it leaves out gravity.
There are other gaps, because most of the Universe is still unknown.
Relativity describes a smooth space, but quantum physics describes a world of jumps.
Usually the two theories do not meet, because gravity is weak for tiny things.
If gravity is like other forces, small messengers called gravitons carry it.
When scientists add up the tiny effects of gravitons, the answers become infinite.
The Planck length is a very, very small size, where quantum gravity should matter.
John Wheeler imagined space as a boiling foam at the smallest size.
At the centre of a black hole, the sums of relativity stop working.
At the Big Bang, everything was squeezed small, and the same problem appears.
In 1974, Stephen Hawking showed that black holes slowly glow and shrink.
We need a new theory that makes relativity and quantum physics agree.

The big idea is simple: replace each tiny point with a tiny loop.

B1B2: Space and time seem simple, but physicists have found that they are strange. This book follows two great theories, and then a bold idea that tries to join them.
For thousands of years, people watched the Sun, the Moon and the planets cross the sky, and they used them to make calendars. The heavens looked calm and regular, like a clock that never ran down.
In 1610 Galileo pointed a new telescope at Jupiter and saw four small moons circling it. He also showed that a ball dropped inside a smoothly moving ship falls just as it would on land.
More than three hundred years ago, Isaac Newton described space as a fixed stage and time as a clock that ticks the same for everyone. On that stage, everything else was supposed to happen.
Legend says that Newton saw an apple fall and wondered whether the same pull reached as far as the Moon. He decided that it did, and that the Moon is always falling around the Earth.
Newton found that gravity gets weaker with distance in a very exact way. If you move twice as far from a planet, its pull becomes four times weaker, and three times as far makes it nine times weaker.
The rules that Newton wrote down explained the tides, the paths of the planets and the swing of comets. Edmond Halley used them to predict that a comet would return in 1758, and it appeared on time.

In the 1840s, astronomers noticed that the planet Uranus was slightly off its expected path. Using only Newton's rules and a lot of arithmetic, they said where a new planet should be, and in 1846 Neptune was found there.
Mercury, the planet closest to the Sun, caused a small problem. Its oval orbit turns slowly, and even after counting every other planet, Newton's rules missed a tiny part of the turning.

Newton's gravity worked wonderfully well, but he never said how it crosses the empty space between two bodies. That puzzle waited for Einstein, and this book follows it from relativity to quantum physics and on to string theory.

In 1676 the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer noticed that the eclipses of Jupiter's moons came late when Jupiter was far away. He understood that this happens because light needs time to cross the extra distance.
Light travels at about three hundred thousand kilometres a second. It crosses from the Moon to the Earth in a little over one second, and it reaches us from the Sun in about eight minutes.

In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell wrote the rules that join electricity and magnetism into one idea. His sums showed that a changing electric and magnetic field can make a wave, and that its speed matches the speed of light.

Maxwell's discovery meant that light is a wave of electricity and magnetism. Because other waves, such as sound and water waves, need something to move through, many scientists believed in an invisible sea called the ether.

In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley sent two beams of light along different paths and compared them. If the Earth moves through an ether, one beam should have been slowed, but they found no difference at all.
Some physicists tried to save the ether with strange ideas, such as objects shrinking when they move. The fixes were clever, but they felt like patches on a coat that was already worn out.
As a teenager, Albert Einstein wondered what he would see if he ran beside a beam of light as fast as the beam itself. He later said that this simple question kept coming back to him for ten years.
In 1905 Einstein was twenty-six years old and working in a patent office in Bern, Switzerland. In his spare time he wrote papers that changed physics, and the first of them was about space and time.
Imagine throwing a ball forward from a moving train. Someone on the platform sees the two speeds add together, but light does not behave in that way.
Einstein built his theory on two ideas: physics works the same for everyone moving smoothly, and so does the speed of light. If both are true, then something about space and time must give way.
Imagine a clock made of two mirrors with a flash of light bouncing between them. Each time the flash hits a mirror, the clock ticks once.
Now let the clock fly past you at high speed. You see the flash take a sloping path, which is longer, and since light cannot go faster, each tick takes more time.
The effect depends on how fast the clock moves compared with light. Cars and planes show a tiny effect, but a clock moving at a little under nine tenths of light speed ticks half as fast.

Muons are tiny particles that are made high in the sky when cosmic rays hit the air. They break apart so quickly that they should hardly reach the ground, but they move so fast that their clocks run slowly, and many arrive.

In 1971 Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew very exact atomic clocks around the world on ordinary aeroplanes. When the flights ended, the clocks differed from a clock left on the ground by billionths of a second, as the theory predicted.

Time is not the only thing that changes when something moves quickly. Anything that moves quickly past you is measured to be shorter along its direction of travel, although the people on board see nothing odd.
Imagine lightning striking both ends of a moving train. A watcher on the platform says they happened together, while a passenger says the front one came first, and neither is wrong.

Pushing an object faster takes energy, and the closer it gets to the speed of light, the more energy each extra bit of speed costs. Nothing with mass can ever reach that speed, so it acts as a cosmic speed limit.

Suppose that one twin flies away at very high speed and then comes back, while the other stays on Earth. The traveller has aged less, and the difference comes from the turn and the journey, which are not the same for both twins.

While two people are moving smoothly past each other, each one sees the other person's clock ticking slowly. This seems to be a contradiction, but it is not, because they cannot compare the clocks without one of them turning round.
In 1908 Hermann Minkowski, who had once been Einstein's teacher, saw that relativity joins space and time into one thing. He called it spacetime, and it has become the stage for modern physics.
Everything that happens is an event with a place and a time. To describe a flash of lightning, you need three numbers for where it happened and one more for when.
Imagine a map with space along the bottom and time running upwards. A person standing still draws a straight upward line, and a person who moves draws a slanted one, called a worldline.
Two observers who move differently will cut this map into space and time in different ways. They disagree about distances and times, but they agree about a deeper quantity that mixes the two.
For any event, light makes a cone of paths that spread out in all directions. Everything inside the cone could be reached by a signal from the event, and nothing outside it could.
Because nothing goes faster than light, an event can only affect things inside its cone. This keeps cause before effect for everyone, so no one can see a result before its cause.
In a second paper of 1905, Einstein found that energy and mass are linked by a famous equation. Mass is a kind of stored energy, and the amount stored is enormous.
A tiny amount of mass holds a huge amount of energy. The Sun turns about four million tonnes of its matter into light every second, and it has done this for billions of years.
In a nuclear power station, heavy atoms such as uranium are split in two. The pieces weigh a very little less than the original, and that small difference in mass appears as heat.

In a particle collider, two beams crash head on, and their energy becomes new particles that did not exist before. Most of the mass of a proton is not made of heavier ingredients, but is the energy of the forces inside it.

In 1907 Einstein was sitting at his desk when he realised that a man who falls freely from a roof would not feel his own weight. He later called this his happiest thought, because it led to a new theory of gravity.
Imagine that you are standing inside a closed lift with no windows at all. If you feel pressed to the floor, you cannot tell whether the lift rests on Earth or is pushed upward in empty space.

In the accelerating lift, a beam of light that crosses from one wall to the other would follow a curved path. Since gravity and acceleration cannot be told apart, Einstein concluded that gravity must bend light too.
A globe on a table shows what it can mean for space to be curved. Two aeroplanes flying as straight as they can follow bent arcs on a flat map, and two travellers walking north meet at the pole.

Special relativity did not include gravity, and fitting the two together took Einstein about eight years. His friend Marcel Grossmann showed him the mathematics of curved surfaces, which Einstein needed to describe a curved spacetime.

In Einstein's picture, a heavy object such as the Sun bends the spacetime around it. The planets are not pulled by a force, but follow the straightest paths through the curved region, which happen to be orbits.
Spacetime bends in time as well as in space. Near a heavy object, clocks run more slowly, and for everyday speeds this slowing is most of what we call gravity.

In November 1915, Einstein finished the equations of general relativity, and he used them to calculate the orbit of Mercury. The answer matched the observed turning exactly, and he said that he was so excited that his heart seemed to skip.

In 1959 two Harvard physicists, Robert Pound and Glen Rebka, sent light up and down a tower about twenty-two metres tall. The light changed by a tiny amount, just as general relativity says it should when it climbs away from the Earth.

GPS satellites carry atomic clocks that tick faster in orbit, because gravity is weaker there. Their speed makes them tick slower, and without both corrections your phone's position would drift by kilometres every day.
Einstein's new theory made a bold prediction: the Sun's gravity should bend the light of stars that pass close to it. The bending should be twice as large as Newton's rules would give.

Stars cannot be seen in daylight, so astronomers waited for a total eclipse of the Sun on 29 May 1919. Arthur Eddington and his colleagues photographed stars near the dark Sun from the island of Príncipe and from Brazil.

When the photographs were compared, the stars close to the Sun seemed to have moved slightly, as Einstein's theory predicted. The news reached the newspapers, and almost overnight Einstein became the most famous scientist in the world.
Gravity can bend light on a large scale too. When a heavy galaxy lies between us and a faraway one, the faraway galaxy's light is bent into arcs, or even a ring.

The idea of a star too heavy to let light escape is older than relativity. In the 1780s, John Michell and later Pierre-Simon Laplace wondered whether such dark stars might exist, but they had no way to be sure.

In 1916, only a few weeks after Einstein published his equations, Karl Schwarzschild solved them for a single round mass. He was serving as a soldier on the Russian front, and he sent his answer to Einstein in a letter.

The solution showed that there is a certain distance from the centre where gravity becomes so strong that nothing can get away. For a star as massive as the Sun, that distance would be about three kilometres.
A massive star that has used up its fuel can collapse under its own weight. If enough mass is squeezed inside the critical distance, the result is a black hole, with an event horizon as its edge.

A traveller falling feet first towards a black hole would feel her feet pulled harder than her head, and she would be stretched. Someone watching from far away would see her slow down, fade, and never quite cross.

Astronomers have strong evidence for black holes, such as the X-rays that pour out near a star in the constellation Cygnus. In 2019 a network of telescopes made the first picture of the glowing gas around a black hole in the galaxy M87.

In 1916 Einstein realised that his equations allowed ripples in spacetime, which we call gravitational waves. They would move at the speed of light, but he feared they would be too faint ever to detect.

In the 1970s, Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found two small, dense stars that circle each other very closely. Over the years their orbit grew smaller by exactly the amount that gravitational waves would take away.

To catch the waves directly, scientists built LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory. It has two detectors in the United States, each with two arms four kilometres long, and a passing wave stretches one arm slightly more.

On 14 September 2015, both detectors recorded a signal that rose quickly in pitch and then stopped, lasting only a fraction of a second. After months of checks, the discovery was announced in February 2016.

The signal had come from two black holes, each about thirty times the mass of the Sun, that spiralled together and merged. This happened more than a billion years ago, and the waves spread out across space until they reached the Earth.

The change that LIGO measured was far smaller than the width of a proton, which shows how sensitive the instruments are. Many more waves have been found since, and in 2017 two neutron stars were seen merging in both gravitational waves and light.

When Einstein applied his equations to the whole Universe, they suggested that space must be growing or shrinking. He did not like this answer, so in 1917 he added an extra term to his equations that kept the Universe still.

In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that almost all galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther away they are, the faster they go. It is not that galaxies fly through space, but that space itself is stretching between them.

If the Universe is expanding now, then in the past everything must have been closer together. Running the story backwards, we find a very hot and dense beginning that astronomers call the Big Bang, about fourteen billion years ago.

In 1998 two teams of astronomers studied distant exploding stars and found something surprising: the expansion of the Universe is speeding up. Scientists call the cause dark energy, but nobody knows what it is.
By 1900 physicists had a problem with hot glowing objects. Their best theory said that a hot poker should give off endless amounts of blue and violet light, but real pokers do not.
The German physicist Max Planck found a way out in 1900. He suggested that a hot object can give out energy only in small packets, and at first he thought this was just a mathematical trick.
Planck found that the size of each packet depends on the colour of the light, so blue light has bigger packets than red. The packets are so small that we never notice them in daily life.

A strange effect was known in the 1800s: when light falls on certain metals, it knocks tiny particles called electrons out of the surface. A bright red light does nothing, but even a dim blue light makes sparks, which the old theory could not explain.

In 1905 Einstein took Planck's idea seriously and said that light itself comes in packets, which we now call photons. A photon of blue light has enough energy to knock out an electron, but a photon of red light does not.
For a hundred years before this, experiments had shown that light behaves like a wave. Two beams of light cross and make stripes of bright and dark, so light seems to be both packets and a wave.

In 1911 Ernest Rutherford showed that an atom has a tiny heavy centre, called the nucleus, with electrons around it. According to the old rules, though, the electrons should lose energy and spiral into the centre in a flash.

In 1913 Niels Bohr proposed that electrons can only sit in certain levels, like steps on a staircase. When an electron jumps from a higher level to a lower one, it gives out a photon of one particular colour.

Every element gives out its own pattern of coloured lines, like a fingerprint. By splitting the light from stars with a prism, astronomers can tell what the stars are made of, even though they are very far away.

In 1924 the French prince Louis de Broglie suggested that if light can act like a particle, electrons might act like waves. Experiments a few years later showed electrons making wave patterns, and he was right.

In 1925 Werner Heisenberg found one way to describe the atom with tables of numbers, and in 1926 Erwin Schrödinger found another with a wave equation. They looked completely different, but they gave the same answers.

In Schrödinger's equation, a particle such as an electron is described by a wave that spreads through space. Max Born then showed that the wave does not show where the electron is, but gives the chance of finding it in each place.

Imagine firing electrons one at a time at a screen with two narrow slits. Each electron arrives at one spot, but after thousands have landed, the spots make a striped pattern that only a wave could make.

If scientists put a detector at one slit to see which way each electron goes, the stripes disappear. Looking at the electron changes what it does, and that is one of the deepest puzzles of quantum physics.
In 1927 Heisenberg stated what is now called the uncertainty principle. The more exactly you know where a particle is, the less exactly you can know how it is moving, and the other way round.

This is not because our instruments are clumsy, but because of how waves work. A short splash has a clear position but no clear wavelength, while a long smooth ripple has a clear wavelength but no clear position.

Before it is measured, a quantum object can be described as being in several states at once, which is called a superposition. When we measure it we always find one result, and the wave tells us only how likely each result is.

Einstein found it hard to accept chance at the heart of nature, and he said he did not believe that God plays dice. Niels Bohr replied that nature does not have to follow our expectations, and the two men argued for years.
In 1935 Schrödinger described an imaginary cat in a sealed box, alive and dead at once until someone looked. He did not mean it as a real experiment, but as a way to show how strange the idea sounds.

Physicists agree on how to use quantum theory, and its predictions have passed every test. They do not agree about what it means, and ideas such as many worlds or hidden guiding waves are still debated today.

In 1928 the British physicist Paul Dirac wrote an equation that combined quantum physics with special relativity. It described the electron beautifully, but it also had a strange extra solution that he could not ignore.

Dirac realised that his equation predicted a kind of mirror-image particle with the same mass as the electron but the opposite charge. In 1932 Carl Anderson found this particle, called the positron, and antimatter became real.

Quantum field theory goes further and says that the basic things in the world are fields that fill all of space. An electron is a small ripple in the electron field, and a photon is a ripple in the electromagnetic field.

In the 1940s Richard Feynman and others worked out how electrons and light exchange energy. Feynman drew simple pictures to keep the sums tidy, and the theory now predicts some numbers correctly to more than ten decimal places.

According to quantum field theory, even empty space is never perfectly still, because the fields keep jittering a little. In 1947 Willis Lamb measured a tiny change in the light from hydrogen that this jittering explained.

In 1935 Einstein and two colleagues, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen, pointed out a strange feature of quantum physics. Two particles can be linked so that measuring one seems to decide the result for the other, however far apart they are.

In 1964 John Bell showed that the link could be tested, and later experiments found that it is real. Entanglement is now a well-tested part of nature, and Alain Aspect and two others shared the Nobel Prize in 2022.
Entanglement sounds like magic, but it cannot carry a message. Each result looks random on its own, and the pattern appears only when the two sets are brought together by an ordinary signal.
Quantum physics is not only strange, but also very useful. The rules of the atom explain how lasers work, how transistors switch currents, and how scanners see inside the body.

Atomic clocks keep time by counting the beats of atoms, and they make satellite navigation possible. Solar cells and LED lamps depend on quantum rules, and engineers are now building the first quantum computers.

Everything that happens in nature comes from four forces, and gravity holds planets in orbit while electromagnetism makes light and chemistry. The strong force holds the core of an atom together, and the weak force causes some radioactivity.

In quantum field theory, a force is carried between particles by a messenger particle. Light is the messenger of electromagnetism, gluons carry the strong force, and the heavy W and Z particles carry the weak force.

In the 1960s physicists learned that protons and neutrons are not basic, but made of smaller particles called quarks. There are six kinds, and a proton is two up quarks and one down quark, held together by gluons.

No one has ever seen a quark alone, because the strong force grows stronger as quarks are pulled apart. Neutrinos are different, because they hardly interact at all, and billions of them from the Sun pass through your body every second.

The electron has two heavier cousins, the muon and the tau, and each has a matching neutrino. The quarks also come in three families of increasing mass, and the reason for this pattern is still a mystery.

All these particles and three of the four forces are described by the Standard Model, which was put together in the 1970s. It has passed test after test, and some of its predictions have been confirmed to many decimal places.

The mathematics demanded that particles should have no mass at all, which is not what we see. In 1964 Peter Higgs and others suggested that an invisible field gives particles their mass, and a ripple in it would be a new particle.

To search for the Higgs boson, physicists built the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, near Geneva, in a ring tunnel about twenty-seven kilometres long. On 4 July 2012, two teams announced that they had found it, and Higgs and François Englert shared the Nobel Prize in 2013.

The Standard Model is one of the great triumphs of science, but it leaves out gravity completely. Gravity is far weaker than the other forces, and nobody has been able to fit it into the same quantum picture.
There are other gaps: dark matter and dark energy fill most of the Universe, and the model cannot say why matter beat antimatter. Physicists therefore think it is only part of the full story.

Relativity and quantum physics both work wonderfully, but they describe the world in very different ways. Relativity sees a smooth, curved spacetime, while quantum physics sees fields that jump and give only odds.

Most of the time the two theories never meet, because each takes charge of a different kind of situation. Quantum physics rules over atoms where gravity is far too weak to matter, and relativity rules over planets and stars where quantum effects average out.

The trouble begins when something is very heavy and very small at once. If gravity follows the other forces, it should be carried by tiny messengers called gravitons, and physicists tried to calculate how they behave.
When these sums are done for very short distances, the answers come out infinite. For the other forces there are clever tricks that remove the infinities, but for gravity the tricks fail.

There is a special distance, called the Planck length, where this trouble should become serious. It is about a hundred billion billion times smaller than a proton, which is far too small to see with any machine we can build.
The American physicist John Wheeler suggested that at this tiny scale spacetime itself might not be smooth. He imagined a restless foam, like the sea seen close up, but nobody has ever observed it.

Inside a black hole, relativity predicts that matter is squeezed to a point of infinite density, called a singularity. Whenever a theory gives an infinite answer, it usually means that the theory is being used where it no longer works.
The same problem occurs at the beginning of the Universe. Running the expansion backward, relativity squeezes everything into a point, and the theory fails just when quantum effects matter most.

In 1974 Stephen Hawking showed that quantum effects make a black hole give off a faint glow, so it very slowly shrinks. This raised a deep puzzle about what becomes of the information that fell in, and it is still debated.

The two great theories therefore fit together awkwardly, like two puzzle pieces that do not quite match. Physicists believe that a deeper theory of quantum gravity must explain both, and the rest of this book looks at one bold candidate.

In 1968 a young physicist named Gabriele Veneziano was studying data about the strong force. He noticed that an old formula from mathematics matched the data surprisingly well, but he did not know why.

In 1970 three physicists, Yoichiro Nambu, Holger Nielsen and Leonard Susskind, each saw what the formula meant. It was the mathematics of tiny strings that stretch and vibrate, and so string theory was born.

As a theory of the strong force, strings did not work well, because they predicted a particle that was never seen. In the mid-1970s the theory of quarks and gluons explained the strong force better, and most physicists moved on.
In 1974 Joël Scherk and John Schwarz took another look at the unwanted particle. It had no mass and a spin of two, which is exactly what a graviton should be, so the theory might describe gravity.

That changed the question, because string theory was now a candidate for a theory of everything, not only of the strong force. John Schwarz worked on it for about ten years, and most physicists thought that he was wasting his time.

In 1984 Michael Green and John Schwarz showed that a serious mathematical flaw cancelled out in one version of the theory. Thousands of physicists then rushed to work on string theory, and the period is called the first superstring revolution.
In string theory, a particle such as an electron is not a point, but a tiny loop of string. From far away, the loop looks like a point, just as a coin looks like a dot from across a field.
The strings are extremely small, about the Planck length, which is far smaller than any machine can see. That is why nobody has seen one, and why testing the theory is so hard.
People often ask what a string is made of. In the theory the string is not made of anything smaller, but is the basic ingredient, just as the point was meant to be.

If string theory is right, then all particles and forces are different behaviours of the same kind of string. That is a bold dream of simplicity, and it is why many physicists find the theory so attractive.
A guitar string can vibrate in many different patterns, and each pattern produces a different note. The simplest pattern gives a low note, and a pattern with more wiggles gives a higher one.
String theory says that a tiny string works in a similar way. Each vibration pattern would be a different particle, so an electron, a quark and a photon are one string playing different notes.

The faster a string wiggles, the more energy it holds, and Einstein's idea that energy and mass are linked means more energy is more mass. So the mass of a particle would be decided by how its string vibrates.

Strings are pulled extremely tight, so most patterns of vibration carry a gigantic amount of energy. Those particles would be far too heavy for any machine to make, and the particles we know come from the quietest patterns.
A string can be an open piece with two ends, or a closed loop with no ends at all. One closed-loop pattern has no mass and a spin of two, the graviton, so gravity is built into the theory.

Strings can break apart and join together, just as a rubber band can be cut or knotted. Two strings can merge into one, or one can split into two, and these simple steps are the interactions between particles in the theory.

In ordinary quantum field theory, two point-like particles meet at a single point, and this is where the infinite answers come from. When two strings join, the history of the event forms a smooth surface with no sharp point to blame.

Another way to see it is that a string has some size, so it cannot be squeezed into an exact point. This may smooth out the wild jumps of spacetime at the tiniest scale, which is where ordinary quantum gravity went wrong.
The earliest string theory had only force particles and some serious flaws. A new rule called supersymmetry added matter particles and cured the worst problems, which is why we speak of superstrings.

In most theories, scientists must measure many numbers, such as the masses of particles, and put them in by hand. String theory is different in principle, because its numbers should come from the theory itself, but nobody has yet managed to calculate them.

In 1919 a German mathematician named Theodor Kaluza wrote to Einstein with a daring idea. If space had a fifth dimension, he said, Einstein's equations would also contain Maxwell's equations for light, making gravity and electromagnetism one thing.
In 1926 the Swedish physicist Oskar Klein made the idea more believable. He suggested that the fifth dimension is curled up into a tiny circle, so small that we cannot notice it in everyday life.
Imagine a tiny ant standing on a long garden hose in a field. From far away the hose is a line, but the ant can also walk around it, so there is a second, tiny direction.

String theory takes this old idea much further than Kaluza and Klein ever did. The mathematics of superstrings only works if spacetime has ten dimensions in all, which means nine of space and one of time.
We see only three dimensions of space, so where are the other six? The usual answer is that they are rolled up into a very small shape at every point of space, much smaller than an atom.

In 1985 Philip Candelas, Gary Horowitz, Andrew Strominger and Edward Witten suggested that the rolled-up dimensions have a special shape. It is named after the mathematicians Eugenio Calabi and Shing-Tung Yau, who studied such shapes earlier.

The shape of a trumpet decides which notes it can play, and the shape of the hidden dimensions would decide how strings can vibrate. The number of holes in the shape, for example, could decide how many families of particles there are.

The trouble is that there is an enormous number of possible shapes, and the theory does not say which one is the real one. Choosing the right shape, one that gives the particles and forces of our world, is a great challenge.

Some ideas suggest that the extra dimensions might be larger than we think. Experiments have tested gravity at distances of less than a tenth of a millimetre and found no sign of extra dimensions so far.
It is important to be honest about the status of the idea. The hidden dimensions come out of the mathematics of the theory, and no experiment has yet shown that they exist.

By the late 1980s physicists had found not one but five different versions of superstring theory. This was an embarrassment, because there is only one Universe and a theory of everything ought to be unique.
Clues began to appear that the five might be related. A surprising discovery called T-duality showed that a string moving on a very large circle behaves exactly like a string on a very small circle.

Other dualities connect theories that look completely different at first sight. A theory with strong forces can look like another theory with weak forces, which gave physicists a new way to explore the strong case.

In March 1995, at a conference in California, Edward Witten made a famous announcement. He argued that the five theories are not separate, but are different views of one deeper theory, which he called M-theory.
One of the surprises was that M-theory lives in eleven dimensions. When the forces in one version are turned up, a hidden eleventh dimension unfolds and strings stretch into larger things.
Nobody is sure what the M stands for, and people have suggested magic, mystery, membrane and matrix. The honest answer is that physicists know only some corners of M-theory, and not the whole of it.

The new picture contains more than strings, because it also has flat, flexible sheets called branes, short for membranes. In 1995 Joseph Polchinski showed that the ends of open strings can be fixed to such sheets.

An open string with its ends stuck on a brane can slide along it, but cannot leave. Closed loops, including the graviton, can float freely away, which would mean that gravity behaves differently from the other forces.

Some physicists have suggested that our whole world might be a three-dimensional brane inside a larger space. If so, gravity could leak into the extra dimensions, and that might explain why gravity is so much weaker than the other forces.
This picture is very much a work in progress. Nobody yet has a complete set of equations for M-theory, and so it is more a promise than a finished theory.

In the early 1970s Jacob Bekenstein noticed that a black hole behaves as if it has a great deal of disorder, called entropy. Surprisingly, this entropy grows with the area of the black hole's surface, not with the space inside it.

Then Stephen Hawking showed that black holes glow faintly, and so they have a temperature. Hot things are made of many small moving parts, which suggested that black holes have inner parts of some kind that we cannot see.

In physics, entropy counts the number of hidden arrangements of the small parts that all look the same from the outside. For a black hole, the numbers were known from Hawking's formula, but nobody knew what was being counted.
In 1996 Andrew Strominger and Cumrun Vafa used string theory to look for an answer. They built a special black hole from branes and counted the ways that the strings and branes could be arranged.
The number that they found matched the earlier formula exactly. That was a real success, but it worked only for certain special black holes, and not for ordinary ones like those in the sky.

Meanwhile Gerard 't Hooft and Leonard Susskind noticed that a region of space seems to hold no more information than fits on its surface. Like a hologram, a flat surface might hold everything about a solid three-dimensional object.
In 1997 Juan Maldacena found a precise example of this idea. A string theory with gravity in one kind of space equals an ordinary quantum theory, without gravity, on the edge of that space.

The space in Maldacena's example is curved like a saddle and is called anti-de Sitter space. Our own Universe is not like that, so the discovery is a model that teaches us about gravity, not a picture of the real world.

The link has proved useful because it turns hard problems into easier ones. Physicists have used it to study hot, tightly packed matter, such as the plasma made in colliders, which is very difficult to calculate directly.

The holographic idea hints at something deep: space and gravity might not be basic, but might grow out of simpler quantum patterns. This is an exciting thought, but it remains a clue and not a final answer.
Supersymmetry says that every known particle has a heavier partner of the opposite kind, so matter particles pair with force particles. None of these partners has been seen so far.
The idea is attractive to many physicists for a practical reason. Quantum effects should make the Higgs boson very heavy, but partners would cancel them and keep its mass at the observed value.

Partners seem to help in another important way, which concerns the forces. Without partners the strengths of three forces almost meet at high energy, but with them the lines seem to meet at one point.
The lightest partner might be stable and have no electric charge, which is just what dark matter needs. If so, supersymmetry would explain something that astronomers have seen but not yet understood.

The Large Hadron Collider has searched for partners for years and has found nothing. This does not prove that they are absent, because they may be too heavy, but the hopes of many physicists have grown dimmer.

Superstring theory has so many possible ways to roll up its hidden dimensions that physicists speak of a landscape of possible universes. Some estimates of their number are as large as one followed by five hundred zeros, although that figure is very rough.
Dark energy is a number that might differ from one universe to another. A simple estimate says it should be about a hundred orders of magnitude larger, which is one of the biggest puzzles in physics.

In 1987 Steven Weinberg pointed out that if the number varies from place to place, then galaxies could form only where it is small. We would live in such a place, because we could not live anywhere else.

The theory of cosmic inflation suggests that space may have grown very fast in the early Universe, and some versions suggest that it never stops. New bubbles would keep forming, each with its own laws, and ours would be only one of them.

Many physicists find this idea unsatisfying, because we may never be able to see other bubbles. Others are working on a project, called the swampland, that may show the landscape is much smaller than it first appeared.

The Large Hadron Collider reaches about thirteen thousand billion electron volts, but strings would show themselves at an energy about a million billion times larger. That huge gap is the main reason why testing string theory is so difficult.

To reach the energy where strings could be seen directly, scientists would need a particle accelerator many light-years across. Nobody could ever build such a machine, so a direct test is out of reach.
Nature itself sometimes makes particles of very high energy. In 1991 a cosmic ray was seen with a record energy, but even that one is still tens of millions of times too small.

There are other ways to look for clues, such as testing gravity at extremely short distances. Careful experiments have measured gravity down to a few hundredths of a millimetre and found only what Einstein predicted.

Some versions of string theory predict that long threads called cosmic strings may stretch across space, left over from the early Universe. Astronomers have searched for their effects on starlight and on gravitational waves, and so far they have found none.

In 2014 a team announced twisting patterns in the glow of the Big Bang, which might have come from waves in the early Universe. Soon afterwards, scientists realised that cosmic dust could explain the signal, and the claim was withdrawn.

Some theories of quantum gravity suggest that spacetime foam might slow high-energy light slightly more than low-energy light. Astronomers have studied flashes of gamma rays from very far away, and they have found no such delay.

Critics such as Lee Smolin and Peter Woit argue that string theory has made no clear prediction that experiments could prove wrong. They fear that it has become a beautiful mathematical structure without a test.
Supporters reply that testing a deep new theory takes time. The Higgs boson was proposed in 1964 and found in 2012, and gravitational waves were predicted a century before they were seen.

A theory that can never be tested is not yet science, and many scientists agree about that. The disagreement is about whether string theory will someday offer a test, and whether it deserves the patience that it has been given.

Whatever happens to string theory as a theory of nature, it has already helped mathematics. One famous example is mirror symmetry, which showed that two very different twisted shapes can give the same physical answers.
The methods of string theory have also been used in other parts of physics. They give new ways to calculate how particles collide, and they help to describe hot matter and some strange materials.

String theory has rivals, and the best known one starts from a very different idea. Loop quantum gravity, from Abhay Ashtekar, Lee Smolin and Carlo Rovelli, pictures space as a net of tiny loops, with area in steps.

There are other ideas too, including causal sets and attempts to rescue ordinary quantum field theory for gravity. None of these approaches has been tested, and no one knows which of them, if any, will succeed.

A growing number of physicists suspect that space itself is not basic. Quantum links between tiny pieces of the world might knit together the smooth space that we see, in the way that threads make cloth.
Time raises some of the deepest questions of all. The basic equations hardly tell past from future, yet we remember yesterday and not tomorrow, which may be linked to how the Universe began.

What happened before the Big Bang, if the question has meaning, is completely unknown. Ideas such as a bounce from an earlier universe or an endless birth of new bubbles are discussed, but none has yet been confirmed.

The history of physics teaches us to be humble about our best theories. Newton's rules turned out to be a good approximation of Einstein's, and quantum field theory may in turn be a good approximation of something deeper.

New instruments are coming, and some of them are already being built. A planned space observatory for gravitational waves, better telescopes and stronger colliders may bring clues that no one has yet imagined.

We now have two wonderful theories of space and time, and a bold idea that might join them. We do not yet know whether string theory is right, and that unfinished quality is exactly what makes the subject so exciting.
C1C2: At night, lying on the grass beneath the stars, space looks like nothing more than an empty stage on which everything else happens. Physicists have found, however, that space and time are far stranger than they seem, and that they can bend, stretch and even blur. This book follows two great theories to the place where they clash, and then looks at a bold and unproven idea that tries to unite them.

For thousands of years, people gazed at the Sun, the Moon and the wandering planets and used their slow, repeating paths to build calendars. The heavens seemed to follow a hidden order, as dependable as a clock that never needed winding. Behind that calm surface lay questions that nobody could yet answer about what space is and why things move through it.

In 1610, Galileo turned a new telescope towards Jupiter and found four small moons circling it, proof that not everything in the sky revolves around the Earth. He also argued that a traveller below the deck of a smoothly moving ship could not tell, by any experiment, whether the vessel was moving at all. That quiet observation would return, three centuries later, at the very centre of Einstein's thinking, although it seemed a mere curiosity at the time.

More than three hundred years ago, Isaac Newton described space as a great fixed stage, and time as a clock that ticks at the same pace for everyone, everywhere. In his picture, the stage was always there, whether or not anything stood upon it, and it never bent or changed. Planets, apples and people were simply actors, moving across it according to rules that never depended on the stage itself.

The old story says that Newton watched an apple fall and wondered whether the force that pulled it to the ground might reach as far as the Moon. His answer was that it does, and that the Moon is held in its orbit because it is always falling towards the Earth while also moving sideways. One law of gravity, he concluded, governs both a piece of fruit and a heavenly body.

Newton showed that gravity weakens with distance according to an exact rule, so that doubling the distance cuts the pull to a quarter, and tripling it cuts the pull to a ninth. This simple pattern, written in the language of mathematics, proved to be astonishingly powerful. With it, a person with pencil and paper could say how a planet or a spacecraft would travel for years ahead.

Newton's rules explained the tides, the paths of the planets and the long swing of the comets through the Solar System. Edmond Halley used them to predict that a certain comet would come back in 1758, and when it appeared on schedule, long after his death, the public was astonished. A theory that could foretell the sky seemed to have reached the very bottom of nature.

By the 1840s, astronomers had seen that Uranus wandered slightly from the path that Newton's rules predicted, as though some unseen body were tugging at it. Working independently, two mathematicians calculated where such a planet would have to lie, and in 1846 a telescope in Berlin found Neptune almost exactly there. It was a triumph of pure reasoning, and it made Newton's theory seem almost impossible to shake.

Mercury, the planet nearest the Sun, then raised a stubborn little problem that Newton's rules could not quite solve. Its oval orbit slowly turns, and even after astronomers had counted the pull of every other planet, a small part of that turning, about forty-three arcseconds in a century, was left unexplained. Some astronomers suggested that a hidden planet closer to the Sun must be responsible, but careful searches never found one.

Newton's gravity worked wonderfully well, yet he admitted that he did not know how one body could pull another across the empty space between them. That puzzle, together with the odd behaviour of Mercury, was the first crack in an apparently perfect picture. This book follows what happened next, through relativity and quantum physics, and on to the boldest attempt to join them.

In 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer was timing the eclipses of one of Jupiter's moons when he noticed that they came later and later as the Earth moved away from the giant planet. He realised that the delay was the extra time that light needed to cross the growing distance. It was the first good evidence that light is not instant, but travels at a finite speed.

Light moves at about three hundred thousand kilometres every second, a speed so great that it would carry a beam around the Earth about seven times in a single second. It crosses the gap between the Moon and the Earth in a little more than one second, and it needs about eight minutes to reach us from the Sun. Nothing in everyday life prepares us for a speed like that, which is why its consequences seem so strange when we first meet them.

In the 1860s, the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell gathered everything then known about electricity and magnetism into a short set of elegant equations. To his surprise, the equations predicted that a changing electric and magnetic field could travel through space as a wave, and that the wave's speed should match the measured speed of light. He concluded, correctly, that light itself is an electromagnetic wave, although nobody yet knew what, if anything, it was waving in.

Every wave that people had studied before, whether in water, in air or along a rope, needs something to move through. Scientists therefore assumed that light also needs a medium, and they imagined an invisible, motionless sea called the ether that filled the whole Universe. If the idea were right, the Earth would be sailing through it as it circled the Sun.

In 1887, in Cleveland, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley built a delicate machine that split a beam of light in two, sent the halves along paths at right angles and brought them back together. If the Earth were moving through an ether, one half should have been slowed a little, and the pattern of light would have shifted. Despite repeated attempts and careful improvements to the machine, they saw no change whatsoever in the pattern of light.

Physicists wrestled with this surprising failure for nearly twenty years, and some of their ideas were extremely ingenious.
