One suggestion was that anything moving through the ether shrinks slightly in the direction of its motion, which would hide the effect. Each fix, however, felt like another patch sewn on to a coat that was already wearing thin.

As a teenager, Albert Einstein asked himself what he would see if he could run beside a beam of light at its own speed. Maxwell's equations seemed to forbid the answer that common sense expected, a frozen wave standing still in space. Einstein later remembered that this puzzle stayed with him for about ten years before the solution arrived.

In 1905, Einstein was twenty-six and worked as a clerk in the patent office in Bern, examining other people's inventions during the day. In his spare hours, he wrote a series of papers that would transform physics, and the first of them concerned the motion of bodies and the nature of light. He had no laboratory, no university post and no assistants, only a clear and very stubborn mind.

Imagine standing on a station platform as a train passes and a passenger throws a ball forward. You would see the ball travelling at the speed of the train plus the speed of the throw, because ordinary speeds simply add. Light, however, refuses to obey this familiar rule, and a beam shone from the front of a speeding train still reaches you at exactly the usual speed.

Einstein decided to trust two principles above all else: the laws of physics are the same for everyone who moves smoothly, and the speed of light is the same for everyone as well, whatever their own motion. If both statements were true, he reasoned, then something in our ordinary picture of space and time had to be given up. He chose to give up the old picture of space and time rather than the two principles that seemed to him so firmly established.

Picture a very simple clock made of two mirrors facing one another, with a single flash of light bouncing back and forth between them. Every time the flash strikes a mirror the clock ticks once, and because the light always moves at the same speed, the ticking is perfectly regular. Einstein used such a device as a thought experiment to discover what his two principles imply about time.

Now imagine that the clock flies past you at great speed, carrying its flash of light along with it. From your point of view, the flash must follow a slanting path, rising from one mirror and arriving at the other further along, and a slanting path is longer than a straight one. Since light cannot go faster to make up the difference, each tick takes more time, and so the moving clock runs slow.

How big the effect is depends on how fast the clock moves compared with the speed of light. At the speeds of cars, trains and aeroplanes it is far too small to notice, but a clock moving at a little under nine tenths of light speed would tick at only half the normal rate. The effect grows without limit as the speed approaches that of light itself, which is why it can be seen only with extremely fast particles.

Muons are unstable particles, created in the upper air when cosmic rays strike atoms, and they last for only about two millionths of a second before decaying. At that rate, nearly all of them should vanish long before they could cross the many kilometres to the ground, yet detectors at sea level register them in huge numbers. Their internal clocks run slowly because they move at almost the speed of light, so they live long enough, from our point of view, to arrive.

In 1971, Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating carried extremely accurate atomic clocks around the world on scheduled airliners, once towards the east and once towards the west. When they compared the travelling clocks with another that had stayed in the laboratory, the readings differed by tens or hundreds of billionths of a second, in line with the predictions of relativity. Part of that difference comes from gravity, which we shall meet shortly, but the experiment was a fine demonstration that moving clocks really do disagree.

Time is not the only thing that responds to motion, since lengths change too. A rod, a ship or a train that moves quickly past an observer is measured to be shorter in the direction of its travel, by exactly the same factor that slows its clocks. Passengers inside the vehicle notice nothing unusual, and to them it is the world outside that looks squashed.

Imagine that lightning strikes both ends of a long train at the same instant, as judged by a watcher standing exactly halfway along the platform. A passenger sitting in the middle of the moving train sees the flash from the front a moment earlier than the flash from the back, and concludes that the strikes were not simultaneous. Neither person has made an error, because the order of distant events depends on the observer's motion.

Pushing an object to higher speed requires energy, and the nearer it comes to the speed of light, the more energy each extra increase costs. The amount needed climbs without limit, so no object that has mass can ever be accelerated all the way to the speed of light. This is why the speed of light is often described as the cosmic speed limit, and it holds for every messenger, signal and spaceship.

Suppose that one twin boards a spaceship, travels outward at a tremendous speed, turns round and comes home, while her sister waits on Earth. When they meet again, the traveller will be younger, because her clocks, her heartbeats and her thoughts all ran more slowly on the journey. The puzzle of why the twins are not symmetrical is answered by the turning round, which only the traveller experienced.

When two observers glide smoothly past one another, each of them measures the other's clock to be running slowly, and each is correct about their own measurement. It sounds like a contradiction, but it never leads to one, since the two can compare their clocks only by bringing them together, and that requires at least one of them to change direction. Relativity is strange to our everyday intuition, but it is, so far as anyone has been able to test, entirely consistent.

In 1908, the mathematician Hermann Minkowski, who had once taught the young Einstein in Zurich, realised that relativity makes the most sense when space and time are joined into a single four-dimensional whole. He called this whole spacetime, and he declared that from then on only the union of the two would keep an independent reality. Einstein was at first unimpressed, but he soon saw that the new language was exactly what he needed.

Everything that happens in the Universe is an event, and each event has a place and a moment. To pin down a flash of lightning you would need three numbers to say where it struck, and a fourth to say when, which is why the combination is called four-dimensional. The numbers themselves depend on who is measuring, but the event itself is a fact on which every observer must agree.

Imagine drawing a map with one direction of space along the bottom and time rising up the page. A person who stands perfectly still traces a straight vertical line, because she stays in the same place while the moments pass, whereas someone who walks away traces a line that leans to one side. Every object in the Universe leaves such a trail, called its worldline, and a life is simply a long and winding path through spacetime.

Two observers who move relative to each other will slice spacetime into separate space and time in different ways, so their grids on the map are tilted with respect to one another. They therefore disagree about how far apart two events are and how long it was between them. Yet they agree about a quantity that mixes the two, which is how the new picture keeps a firm hold on reality.

Around any event, the paths of light spreading outward and backward draw a double cone, one half pointing to the future and one to the past. Everything inside the future half could in principle be reached by a signal sent from the event, and everything inside the past half could have sent a signal to it. The rest of spacetime lies outside, in a region of events that can neither influence nor be influenced by it.

Since nothing travels faster than light, no cause can ever reach an effect lying outside its cone, and so the order of cause and effect is the same for every observer. That is the reassuring side of relativity, because it means that, however strange clocks and rulers may look, no one can witness a result before its cause. Only the order of unrelated events, which cannot affect each other anyway, is open to argument between observers.

In a second paper, published late in 1905, Einstein showed that the energy of an object at rest is equal to its mass multiplied by the square of the speed of light. Since that speed is enormous, the number it produces is enormous too, and the equation says that a speck of matter is a hidden vault of energy. Mass, in other words, is simply energy that is held in place instead of being on the move, and it can be released.

At its core, the Sun squeezes the nuclei of hydrogen atoms together into helium, and the helium weighs very slightly less than the hydrogen it came from. The missing mass leaves as light and heat, which amounts to about four million tonnes of matter every second. Even so, the Sun is so massive that it has burned for about four and a half billion years, and it will keep shining for billions more.

Nuclear power stations use the same principle in a different way, by splitting the nuclei of heavy atoms such as uranium into two lighter pieces. When the pieces are weighed with great care, their total mass is slightly less than that of the nucleus they came from, and the difference appears as heat. That heat drives turbines to produce electricity, a practical outcome of an idea that began as a thought experiment.

In a particle collider, two beams of particles race in opposite directions and collide head on, and the energy of the crash can turn into brand new particles that did not exist a moment before. Energy and mass are therefore interchangeable, and the number of particles in the Universe is not fixed. Remarkably, most of the mass of an ordinary proton is not the mass of its ingredients, but the energy of the strong force that binds them.

In 1907, while still working at the patent office, Einstein had what he later called the happiest thought of his life: a person who falls freely from a roof would not feel his own weight. If he dropped his keys while falling, they would hover beside him, as if gravity had been switched off. The thought was so simple that it took him years to understand how much it contained.

Suppose you find yourself in a closed lift with no windows, and you feel your feet pressed against the floor. You cannot say whether the lift is standing on the Earth, or is far out in space and being pushed steadily upward by a rocket. Einstein turned this impossibility into a principle: locally, the effects of gravity and the effects of acceleration are exactly the same.

Now imagine that a beam of light crosses the accelerating lift from one wall to the opposite wall. While the light is travelling, the lift rises, so the beam strikes the far wall lower down, and its path appears to curve. Because gravity and acceleration cannot be distinguished, light must also bend in a gravitational field, a startling conclusion for a thing that has no mass at all.

A globe on a table helps to show what it means for space to be curved, even though it is only a curved surface in ordinary space. Two aeroplanes that set out parallel from the equator, flying as straight as they possibly can, will eventually meet near a pole, and their routes look like bent arcs when drawn on a flat map. The straightest possible path on a curved surface need not look straight to someone who is not on it.

Special relativity had left gravity out, and when Einstein tried to include it, he found that he lacked the mathematics he needed. His friend Marcel Grossmann introduced him to the geometry of curved surfaces that had been developed in the nineteenth century by Gauss and Riemann. It took Einstein about eight hard years, full of wrong turns, to turn those ideas into a complete theory.

In the theory that finally emerged, a massive body such as the Sun bends the spacetime around it, rather as a heavy ball would stretch a rubber sheet. The Earth is not tugged by a rope of force, but simply follows the straightest path available in the curved region, which turns out to be a closed orbit. Matter tells spacetime how to curve, and spacetime, in its turn, tells matter how to move, so each shapes the other.

It is not only space that is bent, but time as well, and clocks run more slowly the deeper they sit in a gravitational field. For the slow-moving things of everyday life, this stretching of time accounts for nearly all of what we call gravity, and the bending of space adds only a little. A clock on the floor of a building ticks slightly slower than a clock on the roof.

In November 1915, Einstein completed the equations of general relativity, and he promptly used them to calculate the way the orbit of Mercury should turn. The result was forty-three arcseconds a century, precisely the amount that had troubled astronomers for decades, and Einstein said that he was beside himself with joy for days. A theory born of pure thought had explained something that the old theory could not.

In 1959, two Harvard physicists, Robert Pound and Glen Rebka, carried out a test in a tower about twenty-two metres high, sending gamma rays up and down the building. They found that light arriving at the top had changed slightly in its colour, by exactly the tiny amount that general relativity predicts for light climbing against gravity. It was one of the first precise confirmations that time itself runs at different rates at different heights.

Every satellite in the Global Positioning System carries an atomic clock, and each must be adjusted for two relativistic effects that act in opposite directions. The satellite's speed slows its clock by a few millionths of a second a day, while its distance from the Earth's gravity speeds it up by more, leaving a net gain of about thirty-eight millionths of a second. Without that correction, the position shown on your phone would drift by several kilometres every day.

Einstein's new theory made a bold and testable prediction: the gravity of the Sun should bend the light of any star whose rays pass close to its edge. The amount of bending should be a little under two arcseconds, which is twice the amount that Newton's rules would give. Here, at last, was a way to choose between the old ideas and the new.

Since stars cannot be seen near the Sun in broad daylight, astronomers had to wait for a total eclipse, and the best chance came on 29 May 1919. Arthur Eddington led one expedition to the island of Príncipe off West Africa, while another team went to Sobral in Brazil, and both photographed the stars that appeared around the darkened Sun. Their weather was uncertain and their measurements were delicate, but the work was done.

When the photographs were measured and compared with pictures of the same stars taken at night, the stars near the Sun appeared to have shifted by roughly the amount that Einstein had predicted. The result was announced in London in November 1919, and newspapers around the world carried the headline that a new theory of the Universe had triumphed. Almost overnight, a patent clerk who had become a professor was turned into a household name.

Bending of light turns out to have grand uses, because a massive galaxy or a cluster of galaxies can act as a gigantic lens in space. When such an object sits directly between us and a more distant galaxy, the light of the distant one is stretched into arcs, multiple images, or even a complete glowing ring. Astronomers use these cosmic lenses to see objects that would otherwise be too faint, and to weigh the invisible matter in the lens.

The idea of a body so massive that light could not escape from it is older than relativity. In the 1780s, the English clergyman John Michell, and later the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace, reasoned from Newton's rules that a sufficiently heavy star would hold its own light back, and such stars would look completely dark. They had no way of knowing whether any existed, and the idea was soon forgotten.

Only a few weeks after Einstein published his equations in 1915, the German astronomer Karl Schwarzschild found an exact solution that described the spacetime around a single round mass. He did this while serving in the army on the Russian front, and he sent his result in a letter to Einstein, who presented it to the Academy in Berlin. Sadly, Schwarzschild died of an illness a few months later, so he never saw how important his solution would become.

Schwarzschild's solution contains a surprising feature, a critical distance from the centre inside which the pull of gravity is so strong that even light cannot get out. For a body with the mass of the Sun, that distance would be about three kilometres, and for a heavier body it grows in proportion to the mass. At first, physicists thought that this was only a mathematical oddity that nature would never realise.

A star much heavier than the Sun, once its fuel has run out, can no longer hold up its own weight, and its core may collapse inward with great violence. If enough matter is squeezed within the critical distance, the result is a black hole, bounded by a surface of no return called the event horizon. Anything that crosses it, whether a spaceship, a particle or a beam of light, can never come back out.

A traveller falling feet first towards a black hole would be pulled harder at her feet than at her head, and the difference would stretch her out like a strand of spaghetti. To a friend watching from far away, however, her clock would seem to tick more and more slowly, and her image would fade and redden as it hung just above the horizon. The two descriptions look contradictory, but each is correct for its own observer, and nothing in the mathematics is broken.

The evidence that black holes exist is now overwhelming, from X-rays that pour out of gas pulled from a companion star in the constellation Cygnus to the stars at the centre of our own Milky Way. Those stars race around an invisible object in orbits lasting only years, and their speeds show a mass of about four million Suns. Their discoverers shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics, and in 2019 a worldwide network of radio telescopes had already made the first picture of a black hole's surroundings, a ring of glowing gas in the galaxy M87.

In 1916, Einstein noticed that his equations allowed for ripples in spacetime, disturbances that would spread outward from violent events at the speed of light. These gravitational waves would stretch and squeeze everything they pass through, but he suspected that they would be so incredibly faint that no instrument could ever detect them. For a long time, even Einstein himself wavered about whether they were real or only an artefact of the mathematics.

In the 1970s, the astronomers Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor discovered a pair of tiny, incredibly dense stars circling one another every few hours. Over the following years they measured the orbit shrinking by exactly the amount that Einstein's theory said it should, as the pair radiated away their energy in the form of gravitational waves. It was strong indirect evidence, and it won them the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1993.

To detect gravitational waves directly, physicists spent decades building LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, which has two sites in the United States that are about three thousand kilometres apart. Each detector is shaped like a giant letter L with arms four kilometres long, and laser beams bounce back and forth inside them to detect the tiniest change in length. A passing wave makes one arm very slightly longer while the other becomes slightly shorter.

On 14 September 2015, both detectors recorded a signal that rose swiftly in pitch and then stopped abruptly, lasting only a fraction of a second. The team spent months checking that it was not a glitch, an error or a hoax before announcing the discovery in February 2016. When the signal was converted into sound, it was a short, rising chirp, and it opened a new way of observing the cosmos.

The chirp had come from two black holes, each about thirty times the mass of the Sun, that circled faster and faster around one another and finally merged into one. The collision happened more than a billion years ago, far beyond our galaxy, and for most of that time the waves travelled across the Universe before reaching the Earth. In the last fraction of a second, the event gave off more power than all the stars in the visible Universe put together.

The change in the length of LIGO's arms was far smaller than the width of a proton, which shows how astonishingly sensitive the instruments are. Since that first discovery, scientists have recorded dozens of mergers, and in 2017 they saw two neutron stars collide in both gravitational waves and light, which showed that such collisions help to make heavy elements such as gold. Gravitational waves are now a regular and valuable tool for astronomers, who use them as a new kind of sense.

When Einstein applied his equations to the Universe as a whole, they suggested that space could not stay still, but had to be either expanding or contracting. Since astronomers at the time believed the Universe to be static and eternal, he did not like this answer, and in 1917 he added an extra term to his equations, called the cosmological constant, to hold it steady. Other physicists, such as Alexander Friedmann and Georges Lemaître, preferred to take the equations at face value.

In 1929, Edwin Hubble used the great telescope on Mount Wilson to show that almost every galaxy is moving away from us, and that the more distant a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. This does not mean that galaxies are speeding through space, but rather that space itself is stretching, carrying them along with it, much as dots on a balloon move apart as the balloon is inflated. Einstein is said to have regretted his artificial term, and he reportedly called it his greatest blunder.

If the Universe is expanding today, then in the past everything must have been closer together, and the further back we run the story, the hotter and denser the Universe becomes. This leads to a beginning, which astronomers call the Big Bang, that took place about fourteen billion years ago. In 1965, two radio engineers, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, found its faint afterglow as a steady hiss of microwaves coming from every direction in the sky.

In 1998, two teams of astronomers measuring the brightness of distant exploding stars found something that nobody had expected: the expansion of the Universe is not slowing down under gravity, but speeding up. The unknown cause is called dark energy, and, according to the best current measurements, it makes up about two thirds of everything that there is. Physicists do not yet know what it is, and that mystery, as we shall see, may be linked to the clash at the heart of this book.

By the end of the nineteenth century, physicists faced a puzzle about the glow of hot objects, from the red of a poker in a fire to the white of the filament in a lamp. The best theory of the time predicted that every hot body should pour out ever more energy at shorter wavelengths, producing an endless blaze of violet and ultraviolet light. Real pokers do nothing of the kind, and the failure showed that something fundamental was wrong.

In 1900, the German physicist Max Planck found an answer, but one that seemed almost absurd, even to him. If a hot object could emit energy only in tiny, separate packets, instead of in a smooth and continuous stream, then the mathematics matched the observed glow perfectly. Planck regarded this at first as a convenient mathematical trick, and he spent years trying to find a more natural explanation.

Planck's rule says that the size of each packet depends on the colour of the light, so that a packet of blue light carries more energy than a packet of red. A tiny number, now called Planck's constant, links the size of the packet to its frequency, and it is so small that the graininess of energy goes unnoticed in everyday life. The word quantum, meaning a definite amount, gave the new physics its name, and it has been used ever since for anything that comes in separate, countable units.

Another puzzle had been known since the 1880s: when light falls on a clean metal surface, it can knock electrons out of the metal, producing a small electric current. The old wave theory predicted that brighter light should knock them out harder, but the experiments said otherwise, because only the colour of the light mattered. Even a dim blue beam released electrons, while an intense red beam released none at all.

In 1905, Einstein proposed that light itself is made of separate packets of energy, which later came to be called photons, and that each photon hands over its energy to a single electron. A photon of blue light carries enough energy to free an electron, whereas a photon of red light does not, however many of them arrive. For this explanation, rather than for relativity, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921.

The idea of light as particles was troubling, because experiments going back to the early 1800s had convincingly shown that light behaves as a wave. When two beams cross, they create a pattern of bright and dark stripes, which is exactly what two sets of ripples on a pond would do. Light therefore appears to be both a wave and a stream of particles, depending on how one looks at it.

In 1911, Ernest Rutherford and his colleagues in Manchester showed that an atom is mostly empty space, with a tiny, heavy nucleus at the centre and light electrons moving around it. Yet according to the old physics, an electron circling a nucleus should continually radiate energy and spiral into the centre in a fraction of a second. By rights, no atom should be able to exist at all, and yet we are made of them, and so is everything we see.

In 1913, the Danish physicist Niels Bohr proposed a bold rescue: electrons may occupy only certain special orbits, like steps on a staircase, and while they remain on a step they give off no light. When an electron jumps from a higher step to a lower one, it releases a single photon whose colour depends on the height of the drop. This neatly explained the exact colours that hydrogen atoms emit, which no earlier theory had managed.

Each chemical element gives out its own pattern of sharp lines of colour, a spectrum that works like a fingerprint and that sits unchanged in the light of the most distant stars. By passing starlight through a prism, astronomers learned what the stars are made of, and in 1868 they even spotted a new element in the Sun, helium, long before anyone found it on the Earth. The language of atoms, it turned out, is written in light, and astronomers had at last learned to read it.

In 1924, the French prince and physicist Louis de Broglie reasoned that if waves of light can behave like particles, then particles such as electrons might behave like waves. His idea sounded like a flight of fancy, but within a few years experiments in America and Britain showed electrons bouncing off crystals and making patterns just as waves would. Matter, too, had a wave nature, and the stage was set for a new kind of physics.

In 1925, the young German physicist Werner Heisenberg found a way to describe atoms using tables of numbers that were multiplied by strange rules, and in 1926 the Austrian Erwin Schrödinger found a rival description based on a smooth wave equation. The two methods looked as different as a spreadsheet and a seascape, yet they gave identical answers whenever they were tested. Physicists soon proved that they were two views of the same underlying theory, and the combined subject came to be called quantum mechanics.

In Schrödinger's equation, a particle such as an electron is described by a wave that spreads out through space and changes in time. Schrödinger at first hoped the wave was a real cloud of electric charge, but Max Born showed that its meaning is quite different: the strength of the wave at a place gives the probability of finding the electron there. Nature, on this view, deals in odds rather than certainties, and that idea shocked many of the physicists who first met it.

Imagine firing electrons, one at a time, towards a screen that has two narrow slits cut in it, with a detecting plate behind. Each electron arrives at a single spot, like a tiny bullet, but as thousands of them accumulate, the spots build up a pattern of bright and dark stripes that only waves passing through both slits could make. Experiments of exactly this kind have been carried out with electrons since the 1960s, and also with atoms and large molecules.

The result is stranger still when scientists place a detector near one slit to find out which way each electron went. As soon as the path is known, the stripes vanish and the electrons pile up in two ordinary bands, as bullets would. Gaining information about the electron's route seems to destroy the wave-like behaviour, a puzzle that sits at the centre of quantum physics.

In 1927, in Copenhagen, Heisenberg stated the principle that now carries his name: the more precisely you know where a particle is, the less precisely you can know its motion, and vice versa. The product of the two uncertainties can never be smaller than a certain tiny number related to Planck's constant. In a world of bricks and cars the limit is invisible, but for electrons it is decisive.

The uncertainty principle is not a complaint about clumsy instruments but a consequence of the wave nature of matter. A short, sharp splash on a pond has a definite position but no clear wavelength, whereas a long, smooth ripple has a definite wavelength but is spread over a wide area. A particle, being a kind of wave, cannot have a perfectly sharp position and a perfectly sharp motion at the same time.

Before a measurement, a quantum object is described as being in a combination of several possible states at once, a condition known as superposition. When the object is measured, only one of those possibilities appears, and the wave tells us merely how likely each outcome was. How and why a spread of possibilities turns into one definite result is called the measurement problem, and it is still not settled.

Einstein was deeply uneasy about a theory that placed pure chance at the foundations of nature, and he is remembered for saying that he could not believe that God plays dice. Niels Bohr, the leading defender of the new physics, answered that it was not for us to tell nature how to behave. The two men argued about the matter at conferences and in letters for nearly thirty years, and neither convinced the other.

In 1935, Schrödinger devised a thought experiment in which a cat in a sealed box is linked to a single quantum event, so that, according to the rules, the cat would be both alive and dead until someone opened the lid. He did not believe this absurd picture was true, but offered it to show how oddly the theory behaves when it is pushed from atoms up to everyday objects. Today the cat is a famous symbol of the puzzle, and the story is told in classrooms and cartoons around the world.

Physicists agree completely about how to use quantum theory, whose predictions have passed every experimental test for nearly a century. What they cannot agree on is what it means: some prefer to say that the wave collapses when measured, others suggest that every possible outcome happens in a branching set of worlds, and others propose hidden guiding waves. The debate is not settled, and it may not be settled by experiment at all.

In 1928, the British physicist Paul Dirac wrote an equation that married quantum mechanics to Einstein's special relativity, and it described the electron with remarkable elegance. It also explained why the electron has a spin, a built-in twist, that earlier theories had been forced to add by hand. But the equation contained a puzzling extra set of solutions, and Dirac was too honest to throw them away.

After some struggle, Dirac realised that his equation predicted a mirror-image partner for the electron, a particle with the same mass but the opposite electric charge. Four years later, in 1932, the American physicist Carl Anderson photographed the track of just such a particle in a cloud chamber and named it the positron. Every kind of particle, it turned out, has an antiparticle, and when the two meet they can vanish in a burst of energy.

Quantum field theory takes a further step, and says that the basic ingredients of the Universe are not tiny balls but fields that stretch across the whole of space. An electron is a small, localised ripple in the electron field, a photon is a ripple in the electromagnetic field, and each kind of particle has a field of its own. On this view, a particle is something that a field does, rather than a thing sitting in space.

In the late 1940s, Richard Feynman, Julian Schwinger and Sin-Itiro Tomonaga independently worked out how electrons and light should interact according to this new language. Feynman invented a set of simple line drawings, now called Feynman diagrams, which keep track of the sums, and the resulting theory of quantum electrodynamics is among the most accurate ever made. Its predictions for the magnetism of the electron agree with experiments to better than one part in a billion.

In quantum field theory, even a vacuum is never perfectly empty, because the fields jitter slightly and their ripples flicker in and out of existence. In 1947, Willis Lamb measured a minute shift in the energy of the hydrogen atom, a shift that older theories could not explain, and it matched the effect of that restless background. Empty space turns out to be a busy and seething stage, and not a void.

In 1935, Einstein and two younger colleagues, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen, published a paper that described an unsettling feature of quantum mechanics. Two particles can be prepared together so that their properties are linked, and measuring one appears to settle the result of measuring the other, however far apart they may be. Einstein later called this effect spooky action at a distance, and he suspected that it showed the theory to be incomplete.

For nearly thirty years nobody knew whether the argument could be settled by experiment, until in 1964 the Northern Irish physicist John Bell showed that it could. His mathematical test made it possible to distinguish between quantum linkage and any hidden, ordinary explanation, and experiments from the 1970s onward, notably those of Alain Aspect in France, came down on the side of quantum theory. Entanglement is now an established fact, and three of its pioneers shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Entanglement sounds like a hotline faster than light, but nature does not allow it to be used that way. Each person who measures a linked particle sees only a random-looking result, and the pattern of the connection appears only when the two sets of data are compared by an ordinary signal. Relativity and quantum physics, in this respect at least, manage to coexist peacefully, which is one reason many physicists trust both theories.

Quantum physics may be strange, but it is also immensely practical, and a large share of modern technology depends on it. The same rules of the atom explain how a laser produces its pure beam, how a transistor can switch a current on and off, and how the billions of transistors in a computer chip do their work. They also lie behind the magnetic resonance scanners that doctors use to look inside the human body without surgery.

Atomic clocks keep time by counting the natural vibrations of atoms, and their steadiness makes satellite navigation, banking networks and the internet run on schedule. Solar cells and LED lamps also depend on quantum rules, and engineers are now building the first quantum computers, which use superposition and entanglement to tackle certain problems in new ways. Whatever philosophers may say about its meaning, the theory works superbly, and nothing so far has shown it to be wrong in any experiment.

Everything that happens in nature, from the fall of an apple to the explosion of a star, can be traced to four fundamental forces. Gravity guides the planets, electromagnetism produces light and all of chemistry, the strong force glues together the nucleus of an atom, and the weak force drives certain kinds of radioactivity and helps the Sun to shine. Compared with the electric push between two protons, the pull of gravity is weaker by about a trillion trillion trillion times.

In quantum field theory, a force is not something that reaches across empty space, but something that is carried between particles by messengers, a little like two skaters who push themselves apart by tossing a ball to and fro. The photon is the messenger of electromagnetism, gluons carry the strong force, and the heavy W and Z particles carry the weak force. Gravity, if it follows the same pattern, would have a messenger of its own.

In the 1960s, Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig independently proposed that protons and neutrons are not fundamental, but are built from smaller particles that Gell-Mann called quarks. There are six kinds in total, and a proton consists of two up quarks and a down quark, while a neutron has two down quarks and an up quark. Remarkably, nobody has ever caught a quark on its own, because the strong force grows stronger as they are pulled apart.

Another family of particles consists of the neutrinos, which are so light and so shy that they barely interact with anything. Every second, tens of billions of neutrinos from the Sun pass through each square centimetre of your body, and almost all of them continue straight through the Earth and out the other side. Detecting them requires gigantic tanks of water or ice buried deep underground, shielded from every other kind of disturbance.

Ordinary matter is built from just a few particles, namely the up and down quarks and the electron, but nature has made two heavier copies of each. The electron has the heavier cousins called the muon and the tau, and the quarks form three families in all, each family heavier than the one before. Why the Universe should repeat the pattern three times is one of the unanswered questions of particle physics.

All of these particles, together with three of the four forces, are described by a single framework called the Standard Model, which took shape in the 1970s. It has been tested by thousands of experiments, and its predictions have been confirmed to a precision that is hard to match anywhere in science. Few theories can claim to have explained so much while having failed so rarely.

There was one awkward problem, however, because the mathematics of the Standard Model seemed to demand that the carriers of the weak force should have no mass at all, which is certainly not what experiments show. In 1964, Peter Higgs and several others suggested that an invisible field fills the whole of space, and that particles gain mass by interacting with it. If that is correct, then a ripple in the field should exist as a particle in its own right.

To search for the particle, physicists built the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, near Geneva, a ring-shaped tunnel about twenty-seven kilometres in circumference where protons are driven to almost the speed of light and then smashed together. On 4 July 2012, two separate teams announced that they had found a particle with all the properties expected of the Higgs boson. The following year, Peter Higgs and François Englert were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics.

For all its triumphs, the Standard Model has a glaring omission, because it says nothing about gravity, the force that shapes the Universe on the largest scales. Gravity is also by far the weakest of the forces, and every attempt to treat it in the same way as the others, as a quantum field with messenger particles, has run into serious mathematical trouble. We shall meet that trouble shortly, and it is the reason this book exists in the first place.

There are other gaps in our knowledge too, since astronomers find that ordinary matter makes up only about five percent of the Universe, while invisible dark matter and mysterious dark energy account for the rest. The Standard Model also cannot explain why the Universe contains so much more matter than antimatter, nor why neutrinos have the small masses that experiments have revealed. It is a magnificent partial map of the particle world, but it is not the whole territory, and physicists know it.

Relativity and quantum physics are both immensely successful, yet they paint two very different pictures of the world. Relativity describes a smooth, continuous spacetime that curves in response to matter, whereas quantum physics describes fields that fluctuate, jump from one state to another and offer only probabilities. Each theory is nearly perfect in its own territory, and that is exactly what makes their disagreement so uncomfortable.

In most circumstances, the two theories never come into conflict, because each takes charge of a different range of situations. Quantum mechanics governs atoms and molecules, where gravity is utterly negligible, and relativity governs planets, stars and galaxies, where the quantum jitter averages out into smoothness. A physicist can therefore work happily for an entire career without ever needing both at the same time.

Trouble begins when something is extremely heavy and extremely small at once, and then the old division of labour fails. If gravity behaves like the other forces, then it should be carried between particles by a messenger called the graviton, and physicists naturally set out to calculate what gravitons would do. They used the same methods that had worked so well for light and for the nuclear forces.

When the calculations include gravitons interacting at shorter and shorter distances, they produce results that are infinite, and so they say nothing useful. For the other forces, there are clever mathematical procedures that cancel the infinities away and leave sensible answers, but for gravity those procedures break down. This failure convinced many physicists that ordinary quantum field theory cannot be the final word on gravity.

There is a particular length, named after Max Planck, at which the difficulty should become severe, and it is about a hundred billion billion times smaller than a proton. At that scale, the quantum jitter of spacetime itself should become as large as the spacetime in question. No instrument we can build today comes anywhere near probing it, and that is part of why the problem is so hard.

The American physicist John Wheeler suggested that at the Planck length spacetime itself might no longer be smooth, but might boil and froth like the surface of a stormy sea seen from very close, a picture he called spacetime foam. The picture is only a guess, and nobody has observed anything of the kind. It does, however, capture the idea that our smooth, familiar space may be an illusion of scale, like a photograph that turns into dots when you look closely.

The centre of a black hole is one place where the clash cannot be avoided, because relativity predicts that all the collapsing matter is squeezed into a single point of infinite density, called a singularity. A prediction of infinity is usually a sign that a theory is being used beyond its limits, in the same way that an old map fails at the edge of the known world. Only a quantum theory of gravity could say what really happens there, and nobody yet has one that has been tested.

The same problem appears at the beginning of the Universe, because if we run the expansion backward, relativity squeezes everything into a point, just as it does at the heart of a black hole. At that moment the density and the temperature would be so great that quantum effects must dominate, yet relativity knows nothing of them. The origin of everything we know lies in the region where our best theories contradict each other.

In 1974, Stephen Hawking combined quantum physics with relativity in a delicate calculation and found that a black hole should not be perfectly black, but should give off a faint glow and slowly shrink. This discovery raised a deep puzzle about what becomes of the information about everything that fell inside, which quantum physics says can never be destroyed. The puzzle is still being argued over, and it has been a powerful guide in the search for a deeper theory.

The two great pillars of modern physics therefore fit together as awkwardly as two puzzle pieces from different boxes. Almost every physicist believes that there must be a deeper theory of quantum gravity, in which relativity and quantum physics both emerge as limits. It would have to explain what happens at the heart of black holes and at the first moment of time, and the rest of this book looks at the boldest candidate proposed so far.

In 1968, a young Italian physicist named Gabriele Veneziano was studying data from experiments on the strong force, which holds the cores of atoms together. He noticed that an old formula from pure mathematics, devised in the eighteenth century by Leonhard Euler, matched the data in a remarkably precise way. Nobody, including Veneziano, could say why a formula from a different century should describe particles at all.

In 1970, three physicists working separately, Yoichiro Nambu in Chicago, Holger Nielsen in Copenhagen and Leonard Susskind in New York, discovered what lay behind the formula. It was the mathematics of tiny strings, stretched like elastic bands, that can vibrate, split apart and join together, and the particles that people had been measuring were different notes played on them. In this way, string theory was born as an attempt to understand the strong force.

As a theory of the strong force, however, the string model soon ran into trouble, because it predicted a particle with no mass that experiments never found. Meanwhile, a rival theory, built from quarks and gluons and called quantum chromodynamics, explained the strong force better and passed every test. By the mid-1970s, most physicists had abandoned the string idea, and it seemed to be a clever mistake.

In 1974, Joël Scherk and John Schwarz in Paris and Pasadena, and independently Tamiaki Yoneya in Japan, took another look at the unwanted particle that had spoiled the string model of the strong force. It had no mass and a spin of two, which are exactly the properties that a graviton should have, and so the strange extra particle turned out to be the carrier of gravity. The embarrassing flaw had become the most exciting feature of the whole theory, and it changed everyone's view of the subject.

This discovery changed the aim of the whole project, since string theory was now a candidate for a theory of everything, not only of the strong force. Yet the theory was filled with technical difficulties, and for about ten years John Schwarz worked on it almost alone, with a few colleagues, while many of his peers were doubtful that it would ever lead anywhere. Those who stayed with the idea felt that the mathematics was too beautiful to be wrong.

In 1984, Michael Green and John Schwarz showed that a dangerous mathematical inconsistency, called an anomaly, would cancel out exactly in certain versions of string theory. The news spread quickly, and within a few years thousands of young physicists around the world had turned to string theory, in what is now called the first superstring revolution. A neglected corner of physics had suddenly become one of its busiest fields, with new papers appearing by the week.

The central idea of string theory is deceptively simple: instead of treating the smallest ingredients of matter as points with no size, imagine that each one is a tiny, one-dimensional loop of string. Seen from far away, the loop appears to be a point, in the same way that a coin on a distant table looks like a dot, and for that reason all earlier experiments saw only points. Only a microscope of unimaginable power, far beyond anything that exists, could ever reveal the loop.

Just how small would a string have to be in order to have escaped every experiment so far? According to the theory, it is about as long as the Planck length, a hundred billion billion times smaller than a proton, which is the scale at which quantum gravity should matter. This is far beyond the reach of any machine we can build, which explains why nobody has ever seen a string, and why testing the theory is such a challenge.

A natural question is what a string is made of, and the answer is that it is not made of anything. If it were built from smaller pieces, those pieces would be the basic ingredients instead, and the question would only be postponed. In string theory, the string itself is the end of the line, just as the point was supposed to be in older theories, but with the important advantage of having a size.

If string theory is correct, then every particle of matter and every carrier of force is simply a different way in which the same kind of string can vibrate. The electron, the quarks, the photon and even the graviton would all be different behaviours of a single ingredient, a dream of simplicity that physicists have chased for generations. Whether nature has actually chosen this path is a question that nobody can yet answer.

A guitar string can vibrate in many different patterns at once, and each pattern produces a different note. The simplest pattern is a single smooth arc that gives the lowest note, while patterns with more wiggles give higher and higher notes, called overtones. The sound of a guitar is the sum of many such patterns, and the same string can play them all.

String theory proposes that the tiny loops of the theory behave in a similar way, with one string able to vibrate in an enormous variety of patterns. Each pattern would show itself to us as a different kind of particle, with its own mass, its own electric charge and its own way of interacting. On this view an electron, a quark and a photon are all the same string, playing different notes.

The mass of a particle comes from the energy of its pattern of vibration, because Einstein showed that energy and mass are two forms of the same thing. A pattern with violent, rapid wiggles stores a lot of energy and therefore appears as a heavy particle, while a calm pattern stores little and appears as a light one. In this way, the contents of the particle table would be decided by the music of strings.

Strings are believed to be under unimaginable tension, so that even a gentle vibration carries a huge amount of energy. As a result, nearly all of the possible patterns would belong to particles far heavier than any machine could ever create, with masses close to the Planck scale. The particles that we know would come from the very quietest patterns, which have little or no mass.

A string can be an open piece with two free ends, or a closed loop with none, and both kinds are included in the theory. Remarkably, one of the vibration patterns of a closed loop has no mass and a spin of two, exactly the signature of the graviton, which means that gravity is not added to string theory but arises from it. This is the feature that first persuaded physicists to take the idea seriously as a theory of everything.

Strings can also break and join, so that a single closed loop may split into two loops, or two loops may merge into one, and these simple moves play the part of the interactions between particles. The whole of the theory's physics is built up from them, in much the same way that a game of chess is built from a small set of rules. A single basic process, repeated in many combinations, produces the whole pattern of events.

In ordinary quantum field theory, particles are points, and when two of them collide there is a precise point in space and time where the interaction happens, which is where the infinite answers come from. When two strings merge, the history of the event is a smooth, tube-like surface in spacetime, with no sharp corner that could be singled out as the place where things go wrong. Different observers cannot even agree on where, or exactly when, the two strings joined, so no special point exists.

Another way to understand the cure is that a string has a size, and therefore it cannot be squeezed to an exact point, however hard one tries. This is thought to smooth out the wild jumps of spacetime at the smallest distances, the very place where ordinary quantum gravity falls apart. Calculations suggest that the troublesome infinities do not appear at all, which is why many physicists regard string theory as the first consistent quantum theory that includes gravity.

The earliest versions of string theory contained only force-carrying particles, and they were afflicted by an instability that made them unacceptable as a description of the real world. Physicists added a mathematical principle called supersymmetry, which pairs every force particle with a matter particle and cures the worst problems, and the result was named superstring theory. Supersymmetry is a remarkable idea, and we shall return to the question of whether nature actually uses it.

In most theories of physics, scientists must measure a long list of numbers, such as the masses of the particles and the strengths of the forces, and then put them in by hand. String theory is different in principle, because its numbers should come out of the theory itself rather than being chosen, and that is a very demanding standard. However, nobody has yet been able to carry out that calculation in a way that matches the real world, and so the promise remains unfulfilled.

In 1919, a little-known German mathematician named Theodor Kaluza sent Einstein a daring idea in a letter. If space had a fifth dimension, he showed, then the equations of general relativity would automatically contain the equations of electromagnetism as well, and so gravity and light would be two aspects of one thing in five dimensions. Einstein was struck by the elegance, but he hesitated for two years before he helped to publish it.

The idea needed one more step, because we plainly do not see a fifth direction in which we can move. In 1926, the Swedish physicist Oskar Klein suggested that the extra dimension is curled up into a minute circle, much too small for us to notice, and that the circle exists at every point of space. The result became known as the Kaluza-Klein theory, and it left a permanent mark on physics.

A garden hose gives us a simple way to picture how a dimension can hide, even though it is really there all along. From a distance the hose looks like a line with only one direction, but an ant standing on it could also walk around it in a circle, so the surface has two dimensions. The extra direction is there, but it can be noticed only by someone small enough to explore it.

String theory takes this old idea to a far greater extent, because its mathematics hangs together only if spacetime has ten dimensions in total, nine of space and one of time. The original string theory without supersymmetry needed twenty-six, and a later form of the theory, as we shall see, wants eleven. Physicists did not choose these numbers, but found that the sums fail to work for any others.

We see only three dimensions of space, so the theory must explain what became of the other six, which, in the theory, are rolled up into a shape too small for anything we have built to detect. The shape would sit at every point of ordinary space, like a tiny hidden world attached to each position, at a size that might be near the Planck length. Moving in those directions would mean moving through a distance far smaller than an atom.

In 1985, four physicists, Philip Candelas, Gary Horowitz, Andrew Strominger and Edward Witten, proposed that the six hidden dimensions curl up into a shape of a very special kind. These shapes are named after the mathematician Eugenio Calabi, who guessed that they exist, and Shing-Tung Yau, who proved in 1977 that he was right. They are exceptionally complicated, with holes and twists in several dimensions at once, and nobody can draw them faithfully.

The shape of a trumpet decides which notes it can play, and in the same way the shape of the hidden dimensions would decide how strings vibrate, and so which particles exist in our own world. The number of holes in the shape, for example, might determine how many families of particles nature has. The properties of the whole world could therefore turn out to be a matter of geometry, the shape of the unseen.

The difficulty is that there is a vast number of possible shapes, and the theory itself does not say which of them describes our Universe. Each shape gives a different list of particles, with different masses and different strengths of forces, and only a particular one would match the Standard Model. Searching through the shapes for the one that gives our world is like looking for a single key in a mountain of keys.

Some versions of string theory suggest that the hidden dimensions might be larger than the Planck length, perhaps even large enough for experiments to find. Physicists have tested gravity at distances of less than a tenth of a millimetre, and have looked for signs of extra dimensions in collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, but so far nothing has appeared. The experiments have not ruled out the smallest versions, which lie far beyond their reach.

It is important to be honest about the status of the idea of hidden dimensions, which is a conclusion of mathematics and not a result of observation. No experiment has yet shown that they exist, and a sceptic may fairly say that a theory which needs invisible dimensions has a lot to prove. A supporter will answer that the number ten was forced on the theory by its own consistency, and not chosen to be convenient.

By the late 1980s, physicists had found not one but five different consistent versions of superstring theory, known as Type I, Type IIA, Type IIB and two heterotic theories. This was an embarrassment, because there is only one Universe, and a true theory of everything ought to be unique. It was as though someone had searched for the single key to a lock and returned with five.

Hints began to appear, during the early 1990s, that the five theories might be secretly related to one another. A discovery known as T-duality showed that a string moving on a circle of large radius behaves exactly like a string on a circle of tiny radius, with the roles of two different properties exchanged. If so, the idea of a smallest possible size takes on a very different meaning in string theory.

Other dualities, discovered in the early 1990s, link theories that look completely unrelated at first sight. One theory, when its forces are strong, can turn out to be identical to a second theory when its forces are weak, so that a calculation that is impossible in one description becomes manageable in the other. These connections gave physicists a powerful new way to explore the difficult case of strong forces.

In March 1995, at a conference in California, Edward Witten announced an idea that electrified his listeners. He argued that the five theories are not rivals, but are different views, or limits, of a single deeper theory, and he suggested the name M-theory for it. In the following years, hundreds of papers confirmed one connection after another, and the period became known as the second superstring revolution.

A startling feature of this deeper theory is that it lives in eleven dimensions of spacetime, not ten. When the strength of the forces in one version, called Type IIA, is turned up, a previously hidden eleventh dimension unfolds, and the strings stretch into membranes wrapped around it. What looked like an extra detail of one theory turned out to be a doorway to something bigger.

Nobody is certain what the letter M stands for, and over the years people have suggested magic, mystery, membrane and matrix, depending on their mood. The honest situation is that physicists understand only certain corners and limits of M-theory, and the complete theory that is supposed to link them has never been written down. It is a little like knowing five detailed maps without ever having seen the whole continent.

The new picture contains more than strings, for it also has flat, flexible objects called branes, a name that comes from the word membrane. In 1995, Joseph Polchinski showed that the ends of open strings can be attached to certain branes, called D-branes, which are real dynamic objects and not only mathematical surfaces. Branes can have many dimensions, from a simple point to a sheet to something that fills a large part of space.

An open string whose ends are fixed on a brane can slide along it but cannot leave, so everything made from such strings would be confined to the brane. A closed loop, by contrast, has no ends to hold it, so it can float away into the larger space, and the graviton is such a loop. On this view, gravity could behave quite differently from the other forces, because only gravity can wander off the brane.

Some physicists have therefore suggested that the whole of our visible world, with its atoms and light, lies on a three-dimensional brane floating in a larger space. If that is so, gravity could leak away into the extra dimensions, which might explain why it is so much weaker than the other forces. The brane-world idea is imaginative and has been explored in detail, but it remains a speculation without evidence.

It is important to remember, even after all these exciting discoveries, how much of this picture is still unfinished. Nobody has a complete set of equations for M-theory, and many of the objects in it, such as branes, are understood only in special situations, so the theory is as yet more a promise than a finished construction. This unfinished quality is both its great frustration and its fascination, depending on the physicist you ask.

In the early 1970s, the physicist Jacob Bekenstein noticed that a black hole behaves as though it contains an enormous amount of disorder, a quantity that physicists call entropy. Strangely, this entropy grows in proportion to the area of the surface of the black hole, not in proportion to the volume of the space inside it. A bigger black hole has more disorder, and the measure of it is written on its edge.

A few years later, Stephen Hawking showed that black holes give off a faint heat, and so they have a definite temperature. Everything else in physics that has a temperature is made of many small moving parts, and so Hawking's discovery strongly hinted that a black hole has inner parts of some kind that we cannot see. It also gave an exact formula for the entropy, which was a quarter of the area measured in Planck units.

In physics, entropy is a count of the number of different hidden arrangements of the tiny constituents of a system that all look identical from the outside. For a black hole, the total was known from Hawking's formula, and it is gigantic, but nobody could say what was actually being counted. It was a bit like knowing the number of words in an unseen book without having any idea of the language.

In 1996, Andrew Strominger and Cumrun Vafa, working at Harvard, decided to use string theory to look for an answer. They imagined building a special black hole from branes wrapped around the hidden dimensions, and then counted the ways in which the branes could be arranged when gravity was turned down to a weak level. The sums were intricate, yet the count could be done, and the result was a single clean number.

Their answer agreed exactly with the formula found by Bekenstein and Hawking, which was a spectacular success for string theory and one of its first genuine achievements. It must be said, however, that the match was proved only for certain special black holes with extreme properties, and not for the ordinary black holes that astronomers observe. Extending the result to the ordinary black holes of the real sky is still a work in progress, and an active one.

In the early 1990s, the Dutch physicist Gerard 't Hooft and the American Leonard Susskind noticed that a region of space seems to hold no more information than fits on its surface. A hologram offers a good comparison, because a flat plate can contain all the information needed to produce an image of a solid, three-dimensional object. Perhaps the Universe itself is organised in a similar manner, with its deepest facts written on a distant boundary.

In 1997, the Argentine physicist Juan Maldacena found a precise, concrete example of this holographic idea, which astonished the whole community. He showed that a string theory with gravity, in a space of a particular shape, is exactly equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory without gravity, which lives on the boundary of that space. A world with an extra dimension and gravity corresponds to a world with fewer dimensions and none.

The space in Maldacena's example is curved like a saddle and is called anti-de Sitter space. Our own Universe is expanding and has a different shape, so the discovery is not a description of reality. It is a model, a laboratory in which the ideas of quantum gravity can be tested in detail, and it has taught physicists a great deal about how gravity and quantum physics might fit together.

The link has also become a practical tool, because it can turn a hopelessly difficult calculation in one description into a manageable one in the other. Physicists have used it to estimate the behaviour of the hot, tightly packed plasma of quarks and gluons that is created in collisions of heavy nuclei, and to explore some exotic materials. Some results agree remarkably well with experiments, though the connection to real matter is only approximate.

Taken together, these ideas hint at something profound, which is that space and gravity may not be basic features of the world but may emerge from simpler quantum patterns, rather as a picture emerges from a pattern of dots. It is an exciting thought, and many physicists now consider it a leading clue about the nature of spacetime. It remains, for the time being, a clue, and not yet a conclusion, as the best of its supporters are quick to admit.

Supersymmetry is a mathematical principle that says each known matter particle has a heavier partner that carries a force, and each force particle has a heavier partner that is a matter particle. If it were an exact symmetry, an electron and its partner would have the same mass, so the partners must be heavy enough to have escaped every search so far. The principle also makes superstring theory more consistent, which is why supersymmetry has been so closely tied to the story.

Supersymmetry appeals to physicists for a practical reason, one that is connected with the properties of the Higgs boson. Quantum effects should push its mass up to an enormous value, close to the Planck scale, but the real mass is tiny in comparison, and this is called the hierarchy problem. Supersymmetric partners would cancel the large quantum contributions almost exactly, and so they would keep the Higgs mass at the small value that we observe.

A second attraction is that supersymmetry seems to help to unify the forces of nature. Measurements show that the strengths of the electromagnetic, weak and strong forces change with energy, and without partners the three lines almost cross at very high energy but miss. When the partners are included, the lines seem to meet neatly at a single point, which is a delicious hint that the forces share a common origin.

There is a third reason for interest, which is that the lightest partner of all might be stable, electrically neutral and slow-moving. That is the description of dark matter, the invisible substance that holds galaxies together by its gravity, so supersymmetry might solve two mysteries at once. Experiments deep underground have been looking for such particles for decades, and none has yet been found.

The Large Hadron Collider has searched hard for supersymmetric partners since it began operating, and has found nothing, even though it can reach energies of about thirteen trillion electron volts. This does not prove that supersymmetry is wrong, because the partners could simply be heavier than the machine can produce. But it has weakened the argument that they should appear at accessible energies, and many physicists have lowered their expectations.

In string theory, there are so many ways to roll up the hidden dimensions that the theory seems to allow an almost unimaginable number of different worlds, each with its own laws. Leonard Susskind named this assortment the landscape, and some estimates put the number of possibilities as high as one followed by five hundred zeros, although that figure is very rough. Nobody knows which of these worlds, if any, is the one we live in.

One of the biggest puzzles in physics concerns dark energy, the mysterious something that makes the expansion of the Universe speed up. If one adds up the contributions that quantum physics predicts, the answer is larger than the observed value by about a hundred orders of magnitude, which has been called the worst prediction in the history of science. Something seems to cancel nearly all of it, and so far no one knows what that something could be.

In 1987, the American physicist Steven Weinberg argued that if the value of dark energy differs from place to place, then galaxies could form only in places where it is small, and observers could therefore exist only there. In that case, we should not be surprised to find it small, and Weinberg even estimated how large it could be, years before it was measured. This kind of reasoning is called anthropic, and it divides physicists sharply, some seeing it as insight and others as surrender.

The theory of cosmic inflation, which proposes that space expanded extremely rapidly in the first fraction of a second, offers a possible mechanism for producing many different regions. In some versions, inflation never completely stops, and new bubbles of space keep forming, each ending up in a different valley of the landscape with its own physical laws. Our observable Universe would then be a single bubble in a far larger multiverse.

Many physicists find this picture unsatisfying, and they point out that we may never be able to observe any other bubble or test the claim. Others are working on a programme called the swampland, which tries to show that most of the apparent possibilities are inconsistent, and that the true landscape is much smaller than first believed. The debate continues, and the evidence is not yet decisive either way, so a careful reader should keep an open mind.

The Large Hadron Collider can bring particles to about thirteen thousand billion electron volts, which is a vast energy by human standards. Yet the energy at which a string's size would become visible is thought to be about a million billion times larger, a gap that no engineering of the foreseeable future could cross. This is the central difficulty in testing string theory directly, and it has shaped the whole debate about the theory.

If a particle accelerator were built with today's methods to reach that energy, it would have to stretch for many light-years, which is clearly not a project that any civilisation would undertake. Physicists therefore cannot hope to see a string by smashing particles together in the usual way. They must look for indirect traces, which are fainter and much harder to interpret.

Nature sometimes produces particles with extraordinary energy, and in 1991 a detector in Utah recorded a cosmic ray with the highest energy ever seen, carrying about as much energy as a fast-pitched baseball in a single particle. Even this record is still tens of millions of times too small to reach the energy at which strings would reveal themselves. The Universe, in other words, does not hand us a free laboratory in which the strings can be seen with ease.

Other tests are based on the idea that string theory predicts small changes to gravity at very short distances, or the existence of extra dimensions that would alter the pull of gravity at close range. Careful laboratory experiments with delicate balances have now measured gravity down to a few hundredths of a millimetre, and in every case they have found exactly what Einstein's theory predicts. The result tightens the limits on such effects, but it does not rule the theory out, because the effects may be far smaller.

A few versions of string theory predict that very long threads called cosmic strings, left over from the first moments of the Universe, may stretch across space. Such a thread would bend light from distant galaxies in a distinctive way, producing identical pairs of images, and it might also emit sharp bursts of gravitational waves. Astronomers have searched for both kinds of signal with great care, and so far they have found none.

In 2014, a team of astronomers announced that it had seen a twisting pattern in the polarisation of the glow left by the Big Bang, which could have been a trace of gravitational waves from the earliest moments of the Universe. Within months, other measurements showed that dust in our own galaxy could produce the same pattern, and the claim was withdrawn. The episode was a useful reminder to be careful with extraordinary claims, however exciting they may sound at first.

Some approaches to quantum gravity suggest that spacetime foam might delay high-energy light slightly more than low-energy light, so that two photons from the same distant explosion would arrive at different times. Astronomers have studied flashes of gamma rays from billions of light-years away to look for such delays, and they have found none, which already rules out some simple ideas. String theory itself, however, does not clearly demand such a delay, so the failure to see one is not a defeat for it.

Critics, among them the physicists Lee Smolin and Peter Woit, argue that string theory has now had four decades and the efforts of thousands of researchers, yet it has still produced no clear prediction that an experiment could prove wrong. They fear that it has become a beautiful mathematical structure that is not connected to the real world, and that it has absorbed talent that might have been used elsewhere. These are serious objections, and honest string theorists admit as much, even while they continue to defend their work.

Supporters reply that testing a deep new theory takes time, and they point to history for comfort. The Higgs boson was proposed in 1964 and found only in 2012, and gravitational waves were predicted a century before the first one was detected, so patience has been rewarded before. They add that string theory is still being understood, and that it may well turn out to make firm predictions once its structure is clearer.

A theory that can never be tested, many scientists agree, is not yet science, because science progresses by finding where an idea fails. The disagreement is over whether string theory will eventually offer such a test, and whether it deserves the years of patience that it has been given. Nobody can settle that question today, and a reader should be wary of anyone who claims that it is already settled.

Whatever the fate of string theory as a description of nature, it has already left a lasting mark on mathematics. A famous example is mirror symmetry, the discovery that two completely different twisted shapes can give identical physical answers, a fact that allowed mathematicians to solve counting problems that had defeated them for generations. A set of ideas about physics ended up delivering proven theorems about pure geometry, a gift that nobody had expected.

The methods of string theory have also been borrowed by other branches of physics, even by researchers who care nothing about strings. They provide new shortcuts for calculating how particles collide, new tools for studying black holes, and new ways of describing hot, dense matter and some exotic materials. Even if the theory proved not to describe the Universe, it would have been a rich source of ideas.

String theory is not the only candidate, and its main rival is loop quantum gravity, developed by physicists such as Abhay Ashtekar, Lee Smolin and Carlo Rovelli. It pictures space as a network of tiny linked loops, and it predicts that area and volume come in separate steps rather than smooth amounts. It does not attempt to unify the forces, and like string theory it has so far been impossible to test.

There are other proposals as well, among them causal sets, which imagine spacetime as a scatter of discrete events, and attempts to show that ordinary quantum field theory can be made to work for gravity after all. Each approach has its own champions and its own successes, but none has been confirmed by observation. At this stage of the story nobody is entitled to say which of them, if any, will win.

A growing number of physicists suspect that space is not a basic ingredient of the world but something that emerges from deeper, quantum connections. In this view, the strands of entanglement between tiny pieces of reality might knit together the smooth space that we perceive, much as threads are woven into cloth. The holographic examples met earlier in this book give this suspicion some mathematical support.

Time raises some of the deepest questions of all, for the most basic equations of physics hardly distinguish the past from the future. And yet we remember yesterday and not tomorrow, and eggs break but do not unbreak, which many physicists connect with the unusually orderly state in which the Universe began. In some attempts at quantum gravity, time seems to disappear from the equations altogether.

What came before the Big Bang, if the question has any meaning, is completely unknown. Some physicists have proposed that our Universe was born from the bounce of an earlier one, others that an endless process creates new bubbles of space, and still others that time itself began at that moment. These are fascinating ideas, but they are not yet backed by any evidence, and all of them remain open to doubt.

The history of physics should make us humble about even our very best theories, however well they have been tested. Newton's laws were not wrong but turned out to be an excellent approximation of Einstein's, which apply under a wider range of conditions, and quantum field theory may in its turn prove to be an approximation of something deeper. Each great advance has revealed a larger world, and there is no reason to think that the process has stopped.

New instruments are on the way, including a planned gravitational-wave observatory in space, more powerful telescopes and the proposals for stronger colliders. They may bring clues that nobody has yet imagined, as happened with the discovery of the expansion of the Universe, and they might even show how string theory could be tested. In science, the best discoveries are often the ones that nobody predicted, and that is a good reason for optimism.

We possess two magnificent theories, one of space, time and gravity and the other of everything small, and each has passed every test that was set for it. Whether string theory is the missing bridge between them, or merely a useful step on the way, nobody can yet say. Looking up at the stars, you are standing at the edge of the greatest unsolved problem in physics, and perhaps one day you will help to solve it.
